RISKS IN RELATION TO THE FIRST OFFER 
This being the first public issue of Equity Shares of our Company, there has been no formal market for the Equity Shares of our Company. 
The face value of our Equity Shares is ₹ 10 each. The Floor Price, Cap Price and Offer Price as determined by our Company, in consultation 
with the book running lead managers (“BRLMs”), on the basis of the assessment of market demand for the Equity Shares by way of the Book 
Building Process (defined hereinafter), in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations, and as stated in “Basis for Offer Price” beginning on 
page 174 should not be taken to be indicative of the market price of the Equity Shares after the Equity Shares are listed. No assurance can be 
given regarding an active or sustained trading in the Equity Shares of our Company nor regarding the price at which the Equity Shares will be 
traded after listing. 
GENERAL RISK 
Investments in equity and equity-related securities involve a degree of risk and bidders should not invest any funds in the Offer unless they 
can afford to take the risk of losing their entire investment. Bidders are advised to read the risk factors carefully before taking an 
investment decision in the Offer. For taking an investment decision, bidders must rely on their own examination of our Company, our 
Business, our Management and the Offer, including the risks involved. The Equity Shares in the Offer have not been recommended or 
approved by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”), nor does SEBI guarantee the accuracy or adequacy of the contents of 
this Draft Red Herring Prospectus. Specific attention of the bidders is invited to “Risk Factors” beginning on page 26. 
ABSOLUTE RESPONSIBILITY OF OUR COMPANY’S AND PROMOTER GROUP SELLING SHAREHOLDERS

Our Company, having made all reasonable inquiries, accepts responsibility for and confirms that this Draft Red Herring Prospectus 
contains all information with regard to our Company and the Offer, which is material in the context of the Offer, that the information 
contained in this Draft Red Herring Prospectus is true and correct in all material aspects and is not misleading in any material respect, that 
the opinions and intentions expressed herein are honestly held and that there are no other facts, the omission of which makes this Draft Red 
Herring Prospectus as a whole or any of such information or the expression of any such opinions or intentions misleading in any material 
respect.  
 
Further, each of the Promoter Group Selling Shareholders, severally and not jointly, accept responsibility for and confirms only statements 
expressly made or confirmed by such Promoter Group Selling Shareholder in this Draft Red Herring Prospectus to the extent such statements 
are solely in relation to itself and its respective portion of the Offered Shares and assumes responsibility that such statements are true and 
correct in all material respects and not misleading in any material respect. No Selling Shareholder assumes responsibility for any other 
statement, disclosure and undertaking, including without limitation any and all of the statements, disclosures and undertakings made or 
confirmed by or relating to our Company or its business, or any other Selling Shareholder or any other person(s) in this Draft Red Herring 
Prospectus. 
LISTING 
The Equity Shares to be offered through the Red Herring Prospectus are proposed to be listed on the Stock Exchanges being BSE Limited 
(“BSE”) and National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE” together with BSE, the “Stock Exchanges”). For the purposes of the

Our Company was originally incorporated as ‘Maharashtra Oil Extractions Limited’ as a public limited company under the Companies Act, 1956, pursuant to a certificate of incorporation dated November 21, 1995, issued by Registrar of Companies, 
Maharashtra at Bombay. Our Company was also issued a certificate for commencement of business on January 4, 1996, by the RoC. Subsequently, our Company was converted into a private limited company pursuant to a special resolution passed by our 
Shareholders on February 16, 1998, and the name of our Company was changed to ‘Maharashtra Oil Extractions Private Limited’ and consequently, a fresh certificate of incorporation was issued by the RoC on June 10, 1998. Subsequently, the name of 
our Company was changed to its present name i.e. ‘Maharashtra Oil Extractions Limited’ upon conversion of our Company into a public limited company pursuant to a special resolution passed by our Shareholders on December 28, 2024, and the fresh 
certificate of incorporation was issued by the Registrar of Companies, Central Processing Centre on March 10, 2025. For further details in relation to the changes in the name and registered office of our Company, see section titled “History and Certain 
Corporate Matters – Brief history of our Company, - and Changes in the registered office of our Company” on page 320.

EMPLOYEES (AS DEFINED HEREINAFTER) BIDDING IN THE EMPLOYEE RESERVATION PORTION (“EMPLOYEE DISCOUNT”).

CIRCULATION, ALL EDITIONS OF [●], A HINDI LANGUAGE NATIONAL DAILY NEWSPAPER WITH WIDE CIRCULATION AND ALL EDITIONS OF [●], A MARATHI LANGUAGE DAILY NEWSPAPER WITH WIDE

BID/OFFER OPENING DATE AND SHALL BE MADE AVAILABLE TO THE STOCK EXCHANGES FOR THE PURPOSE OF UPLOADING ON THEIR RESPECTIVE WEBSITES IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE SECURITIES AND 
EXCHANGE BOARD OF INDIA (ISSUE OF CAPITAL AND DISCLOSURE REQUIREMENTS) REGULATIONS, 2018, AS AMENDED (THE “SEBI ICDR REGULATIONS”). 
In case of any revision in the Price Band, the Bid/ Offer Period shall be extended for at least three additional Working Days after such revision of the Price Band, subject to the total Bid/Offer Period not exceeding 10 Working Days. In cases of force 
majeure, banking strike or similar unforeseen circumstances, our Company in consultation with the BRLMs, for reasons to be recorded in writing, extend the Bid / Offer Period for a minimum of one Working Day, subject to the Bid/ Offer Period not 
exceeding 10 Working Days. Any revision in the Price Band, and the revised Bid/ Offer Period, if applicable, shall be widely disseminated by notification to the Stock Exchanges by issuing a public notice and also by indicating the change on the website 
of the BRLMs and at the terminals of the members of the Syndicate and by intimation to the Self-Certified Syndicate Banks (“SCSBs”) and other Designated Intermediaries and Sponsor Bank(s) (defined hereinafter), as applicable. 
The Offer is being made in terms of Rule 19(2)(b) of the Securities Contracts (Regulation) Rules, 1957, as amended (the “SCRR”), read with Regulation 31 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. The Offer is being made in accordance with Regulation 6(1) of 
the SEBI ICDR Regulations, through the Book Building Process wherein not more than 50% of the Net Offer shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis to Qualified Institutional Buyers (“QIBs”) (such portion referred to as “QIB 
Portion”), provided that our Company in consultation with the BRLMs, may allocate up to 60% of the Net QIB Portion to Anchor Investors on a discretionary basis in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations (the “Anchor Investor Portion”), out 
of which of which 40% shall be reserved as under: (i) 33.33%for domestic Mutual Funds; and (ii) 6.67% for Life Insurance Companies and Pension Funds, subject to valid Bids being received from domestic Mutual Funds, Life Insurance Companies and 
Pension Funds, at or above the price at which allocation is made to Anchor Investors (“Anchor Investor Allocation Price”), in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations. Any under-subscription in the reserved category specified in clause (ii) above, 
may be allocated to domestic Mutual Funds. In the event of under-subscription or non-allocation in the Anchor Investor Portion, the balance Equity Shares shall be added to the QIB Portion (excluding the Anchor Investor Portion) (the “Net QIB 
Portion”). Further, 5% of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis to Mutual Funds only, and the remainder of the Net QIB Portion shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis to all QIB Bidders (other 
than Anchor Investors), including Mutual Funds, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Offer Price. However, if the aggregate demand from Mutual Funds is less than 5% of the Net QIB Portion, the balance Equity Shares available for 
allocation in the Mutual Fund Portion will be added to the remaining Net QIB Portion for proportionate allocation to all QIBs. Further, not less than 15% of the Net Offer shall be available for allocation on a proportionate basis to Non-Institutional 
Investors out of which (a) one-third of such portion shall be reserved for applicants with application size of more than ₹ 0.20 million and up to ₹ 1.00 million ; and (b) two third of such portion shall be reserved for applicants with application size of more 
than ₹ 1.00 million, provided that the unsubscribed portion in either of such sub-categories may be allocated to applicants in the other sub-category of Non-Institutional Investors in accordance with the SEBI (ICDR) Regulations, subject to valid Bids 
being received at or above the Offer Price and not less than 35% of the Net Offer shall be available for allocation to Retail Individual Investors in accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations, subject to valid Bids being received at or above the Offer 
Price (“Retail Portion”). Further, Equity Shares will be allocated on a proportionate basis to Eligible Employees (as defined hereinafter) bidding under the Employee Reservation Portion, subject to valid Bids being received from them at or above the 
Offer Price (net of Employee Discount, if any). All potential Bidders (except Anchor Investors) are required to mandatorily use the Application Supported by Blocked Amount (“ASBA”) process providing details of their respective ASBA accounts, and 
UPI ID (in case of UPI Bidders using the UPI mechanism), in which the corresponding Bid Amounts will be blocked by the SCSBs or by the Sponsor Bank(s) under the UPI Mechanism, as applicable, to the extent of the respective Bid Amounts. Anchor 
Investors are not permitted to participate in the Anchor Investor Portion of the Offer through the ASBA process. For further details, see section titled ‘Offer Procedure’ on page 508.

Definition 
1.  
Adjusted Net Debt to Adjusted 
Equity 
Adjusted Net Debt to Adjusted Equity Ratio is calculated as total 
interest bearing loans and borrowings less cash and cash equivalents 
and bank balances other than cash and cash equivalents divided by 
total equity attributable to the owners of the Company, comprising 
equity share capital, convertible preference shares, if any and other 
equity, as reported in the Restated Statement of Assets and 
Liabilities, and excludes non-controlling interest. 
2.  
Capacity Utilization 
Capacity Utilization is derived as a percentage obtained by dividing 
Actual Capacity utilized during the relevant financial year divided 
by the Total Installed / Operating Capacity of the respective facility 
/ plant, as applicable. 
3.  
EBITDA 
EBITDA is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the period / 
fiscal year, plus finance costs, total taxes, and depreciation and 
amortisation expense less other income. 
4.  
EBITDA margin 
EBITDA margin refers to the percentage derived by dividing 
EBITDA by Revenue from Operations 
5.  
EPS (basic and diluted) 
Earnings per share (EPS) equals profit for the year attributable to 
the shareholders of the company divided by the Weighted average 
number of Equity Shares outstanding during the year and giving 
effect to Bonus Issuance. Since there is no dilutive capital, Basic 
and Diluted EPS would be same. 
6.  
Installed Storage Capacity 
Storage Capacity is the total installed capacity of a particular type 
of storage unit in metric tonnes 
7.  
Interest coverage ratio 
Interest coverage ratio is calculated by dividing EBIT by Finance 
Costs. EBIT, i.e, Earnings before Interest and Taxes, is calculated 
as restated profit / (loss) for the period / year, plus finance costs and 
total taxes 
8.  
Inventory Days 
Inventory days are calculated as Average Inventory divided by 
Revenue from operations and multiplied by number of days in the 
fiscal year. Average Inventory is the sum of opening and closing 
balance of Inventory for relevant fiscal divided by two. 
9.  
Net Asset Value per Equity Share 
Net Asset Value per Equity Share (NAV) is calculated as Net 
Worth divided by the number of equity shares outstanding as at the 
end of the year  
10.  
No. of Employees 
No. of Employees means the aggregate number of permanent 
employees employed by our Company during the respective 
financial years 
11.  
PAT margin 
PAT Margin is calculated as percentage derived by dividing profit 
for the period/ fiscal year by Total Income. 
12.  
Profit after tax (PAT) 
Profit after tax (PAT) means restated profit / (loss) for the 
period/financial year as appearing in the Restated consolidated 
financial Information. 
13.  
Return on Capital Employed 
(ROCE) 
Return on capital employed (ROCE) is calculated as EBIT divided 
by closing capital employed for the period / fiscal year. Earnings 
before Interest and Taxes (EBIT) is calculated as restated profit / 
(loss) for the period / fiscal year, plus finance costs and total taxes. 
Capital employed is the sum of total equity plus debt consisting of 
borrowings and lease liabilities plus deferred tax liabilities less 
deferred tax assets, as appearing in the Restated Financial 
Information. 
14.  
Return on Net Worth (RONW) 
Return on Net Worth is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the 
period / year divided by average net worth. Net Worth is calculated

The availability, quality and pricing of our raw materials are influenced by several factors beyond our control, 
including weather conditions, crop yields, natural disasters, changes in cultivation patterns, global and domestic 
demand-supply dynamics, commodity price fluctuations, government policies, logistics constraints and other 
market conditions. In particular, the availability and pricing of soybean seeds are significantly impacted by 
agricultural output and harvesting conditions. Adverse weather events, crop failures, reduced acreage under 
cultivation, diversion of agricultural land to alternative crops, or hoarding by farmers and traders may adversely 
affect supply and increase procurement costs. Further, domestic soybean prices are influenced by international 
commodity markets, global supply-demand dynamics, trade restrictions and pricing trends, making the Indian 
soybean market susceptible to global agricultural and economic developments. 
 
We do not enter into long-term supply agreements for the procurement of a significant portion of our raw 
materials and generally source such materials through third-party suppliers or the open market. Accordingly, our 
procurement arrangements are largely based on individual purchase orders and prevailing market conditions. 
While we have established relationships with multiple suppliers and seek to diversify our sourcing base to 
mitigate supply risks, there can be no assurance that adequate quantities of raw materials, packaging materials or 
other consumables will continue to be available on commercially acceptable terms or at all. 
 
We are also exposed to risks arising from supply disruptions, delays in procurement, supplier defaults and 
volatility in the prices of raw materials, packaging materials and other consumables. Competition for 
procurement of these inputs may further result in increased costs. Any significant increase in input costs may 
not be capable of being passed on to our customers in a timely manner, or at all, due to competitive and market 
factors. Further, owing to the time lag between the procurement of raw materials and the sale of our finished 
products, fluctuations in input costs may adversely affect our margins and profitability. Similar risks apply to 
our trading operations, where market movements may impact pricing and margins.

28 
 
In addition, our suppliers may choose to prioritize supplies to other customers, including our competitors, which 
could affect the availability of critical inputs. Any shortage, interruption, delay or significant increase in the cost 
of raw materials, packaging materials or other consumables could disrupt our manufacturing operations, 
increase our cost of production, adversely affect product availability and pricing, and reduce demand for our 
products. This may, in turn, adversely affect our business, competitive position, results of operations, financial 
condition and cash flows. 
 
While we have not experienced any material disruption in the supply of raw materials, packaging materials or 
other consumables during Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, we cannot assure you that such disruptions, delays or 
adverse price movements will not occur in the future. Any such occurrence could have a material adverse effect 
on our business, results of operations, financial condition and cash flows.

disruption in supply of electricity, may impact our operations and quality of our products. We face power 
shutdown occasionally. To meet such disruptions, we have installed a solar power plant at Gangakhed

Our revenues are substantially dependent on the sale of refined vegetable oils which contributed to 
44.33%, 40.19% and 34.48% of sale of products, in Fiscal 2026, Fiscal 2025 and Fiscal 2024 
respectively, and our inability to anticipate and respond to changing consumer preferences, market

Our revenues are significantly dependent on the sale of refined vegetable oils. We manufacture and sell refined 
soybean oil, cottonseed oil in the domestic market and market sunflower oil, in packaged forms, under our 
flagship brand, “Murli”. For Fiscal 2026, 2025 and 2024, sales of refined vegetable oils contributed ₹9,778.37 
million, ₹7,561.79 million and ₹6,010.80 million representing 44.33%, 40.19% and 34.48%, respectively, of our 
sale of products. Consequently, any reduction in demand for refined vegetable oils could have a material 
adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows. 
 
The success of our business depends on our ability to anticipate, identify and respond effectively to evolving 
consumer preferences, demographic trends, purchasing patterns and product requirements. Consumer 
preferences are influenced by a variety of factors, including changing lifestyles, health and wellness trends, 
increasing awareness regarding nutrition and sustainability, economic conditions, technological developments

38 
 
and evolving market dynamics. Growing consumer preference for alternative edible oils or other perceived 
healthier substitutes may adversely affect demand for our products. If our product offerings, branding initiatives 
or marketing strategies fail to align with changing consumer expectations or do not adequately resonate with our 
target customer base, demand for our products may decline. 
 
In addition, consumers are increasingly influenced by sustainability and social responsibility considerations 
when making purchasing decisions. Any failure to adapt to such expectations may adversely affect the 
perception, reputation and appeal of our brands. Economic downturns, inflationary pressures or periods of 
financial uncertainty may also result in reduced consumer spending and heightened price sensitivity, leading 
consumers to shift to lower-priced alternatives or competing products. 
 
The edible oil industry is highly competitive and continuously evolving. The market is characterized by the 
introduction of new products, the entry of new competitors, increasing product innovation and changing 
consumer preferences. Our continued growth depends on our ability to introduce new products, improve 
existing products and diversify our portfolio in a timely and cost-effective manner. However, there can be no 
assurance that our product development initiatives will be successful, completed within anticipated timelines or 
budgets, or gain market acceptance. Even if successfully developed, newly launched or enhanced products may 
fail to achieve expected sales volumes or profitability. Furthermore, existing or future competitors may develop 
products that are similar or superior to ours or may respond more effectively to market developments and 
consumer trends. 
 
Product development and commercialization involve significant uncertainties, including difficulties in 
forecasting consumer acceptance, estimating time-to-market and assessing commercial viability. We may be 
required to discontinue or abandon certain development initiatives after incurring substantial expenditure if such 
initiatives are no longer commercially feasible. Any failure in developing, launching or commercializing new 
products may adversely affect our growth strategy, customer acquisition efforts, market share and profitability. 
 
As part of our growth strategy, we intend to expand our product portfolio and strengthen our presence across 
existing and new geographies, particularly in tier 2, tier 3 and smaller cities, by increasing the number of retail 
touchpoints where our products are available. Such expansion may increase the complexity of our operations 
and make it more challenging to maintain consistent product quality, brand standards and customer experience. 
There can be no assurance that consumer confidence in our products and brands will be maintained. Any 
deterioration in product quality, inconsistency in customer experience, or failure to meet consumer expectations 
may adversely affect our reputation, customer relationships and market position. 
 
To remain competitive, we must continuously monitor changes in consumer preferences, invest in new 
technologies, processes and product innovation, maintain product quality standards and respond effectively to 
evolving market conditions and regulatory requirements. Any failure or delay in identifying market trends, 
adapting our business strategies, maintaining product quality, responding to competitive pressures or complying 
with changing regulatory requirements may materially and adversely affect our business, prospects, financial 
condition, results of operations and cash flows. Additionally, unforeseen shifts in consumer demand or changes 
in governmental policies and regulations applicable to our products or industry may adversely affect our 
operations, liquidity and future growth prospects.

We face significant competitive pressures in our business. Our inability to compete effectively would 
be detrimental to our business and prospects for future growth. 
 
We face significant competition from other manufacturers, processors, marketers and suppliers of refined 
vegetable oils and soya related products. For further details, see “Industry Overview” and “Our Business - 
Competition” on pages 193 and 308, respectively. Our ability to maintain and grow our market position depends 
on our ability to compete effectively with established industry participants as well as new entrants. Any inability 
to do so could materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows 
and growth prospects. 
 
The markets in which we operate are highly competitive and are influenced by several factors, including product 
quality, pricing, brand recognition, distribution reach and customer relationships. We primarily compete on the 
basis of: 
 
• 
product quality and consistency; 
• 
competitive pricing; 
• 
reliability of supply; and 
• 
brand recognition and customer loyalty. 
 
There can be no assurance that we will continue to remain competitive in these areas. Although we continuously 
seek to strengthen our manufacturing capabilities, improve operational efficiencies, enhance product quality and 
optimize costs, such efforts may not be successful. Many of our existing and potential competitors may possess 
substantially greater financial, operational, manufacturing, marketing, distribution and branding resources or 
other attributes, than we do, enabling them to achieve economies of scale, expand their market presence, 
introduce new products more rapidly or offer products at more competitive prices. Further, domestic processors 
face competition from imported edible oils as well as soybean meal and other processed soybean products. 
When international prices are favourable, imported products can become competitive with domestically 
produced products, putting pressure on domestic realisations. This is particularly relevant for processors 
operating with higher procurement, logistics or processing costs than international suppliers (source: CARE 
Report). 
 
In addition, intensified competition may result in pricing pressures, reduced profit margins, loss of market share, 
increased marketing and promotional expenditure, and a decline in customer retention. If we are unable to 
compete effectively against our competitors, maintain our market position or respond adequately to changing 
market conditions, our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows and prospects could be 
materially and adversely affected. 
 
Further, the edible oil industry is characterized by the presence of a large unorganized sector, which may create 
additional competitive challenges for organized market participants. Unorganized players often compete 
primarily on price, which may exert significant downward pressure on market prices and profit margins. In 
addition, certain participants in the unorganized sector may procure lower-quality raw materials or adopt less 
stringent quality standards, enabling them to offer products at lower prices. Such practices may intensify 
competition and adversely affect the ability of organized industry participants, including us, to maintain market 
share and profitability. Any increase in competitive pressures from organized or unorganized market 
participants may materially and adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations and 
prospects.

Our financial results are subject to seasonal variations and cyclical nature of the industry including 
fluctuations in demand, raw material prices, consumables, finished goods, and overall economic 
conditions, which may cause our revenues and profitability to vary from period to period. 
 
The soybean processing industry is highly dependent on the timely and adequate availability of soybeans, which 
is influenced by seasonal production patterns, monsoon performance, and acreage under cultivation. Any 
fluctuation in crop output due to adverse weather conditions, pest attacks, or shifts in farmer preference toward 
other remunerative crops can lead to raw material shortages. Limited domestic availability often results in 
higher procurement costs or increased reliance on imports, which may not always be viable due to import duties 
and global price volatility. Such disruptions can affect capacity utilization and profitability for processors 
(Source: CARE Report). Our revenues and results may be affected by seasonal factors as well as the cyclical 
nature of our business. We purchase soyabean seeds primarily between October and March coinciding with 
harvest season of the soyabean and demand for our products may fluctuate due to seasonal consumption 
patterns, monsoon conditions, festivals, agricultural cycles, and overall economic conditions. Further, cyclical 
factors, such as changes in industry capacity, customer demand, raw material, consumables, finished goods, 
equipments, price volatility, and broader economic cycles may also impact our performance. While our financial 
performance in past has reflected the impact of such seasonal and cyclical factors resulting into higher revenue 
and profit, there can be no assurance that similar trends will continue and no adverse effect on our revenues, 
margins and financial results in the future due to volatile nature of our revenue and profit. Consequently, our 
revenues, margins and financial results may vary significantly from period to period, and past performance may 
not be indicative of future results.

Our operations involve the handling, storage, processing and transportation of substantial quantities 
of soybeans, soybean oil, soybean meal and other soybean-based products, and any spillage, leakage, 
contamination or loss during these activities could result in wastage of raw materials or finished 
products, damage to inventory and equipment, operational disruptions, environmental or safety 
liabilities and additional costs, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results 
of operations and cash flows. 
 
We handle and process substantial quantities of soybeans and soybean-derived products at various stages of our 
operations, including during receipt of raw materials, unloading, internal movement, storage, processing, 
packaging, loading and transportation. Such activities may result in spillage, leakage, breakage, product loss or 
wastage due to equipment malfunction, failure of handling systems, conveyor or pipeline leakages, inadequate 
storage conditions, human error, improper handling, transportation incidents or other operational factors. 
Soybeans and soybean-derived products may also be susceptible to deterioration arising from moisture, 
infestation, contamination, improper storage conditions, inadequate ventilation or prolonged storage. Any such 
deterioration or contamination may adversely affect the quality and quantity of our raw materials or finished 
products and may require us to incur additional costs for segregation, disposal, reprocessing, cleaning, 
replacement or other remedial measures. Such losses may also reduce the availability of usable inventory for our 
production requirements and adversely affect our ability to meet customer orders. Our operations involve the 
use of storage facilities, silos, tanks, conveyors, pipelines, elevators, loading and unloading equipment and other 
material-handling infrastructure. Any failure, breakdown or inadequate maintenance of such infrastructure may 
increase the likelihood of spillage or product losses and may also cause temporary suspension or disruption of 
our operations. In addition, spillage during loading, unloading or transportation may result in loss of inventory, 
delays in deliveries, damage to vehicles or infrastructure and claims or disputes with customers, suppliers, 
transporters or other counterparties. 
 
Further, significant spillage, leakage or improper disposal of soybean products, edible oils or other materials 
may result in environmental, health and safety concerns and may subject us to additional expenditure, 
remediation costs, regulatory actions, penalties or claims, as applicable under applicable laws and regulations. 
Any accident, fire or other incident associated with the storage or handling of soybean-derived products may 
further result in damage to our facilities, inventory or equipment, employee injuries or operational disruptions. 
Although we undertake measures to minimise handling and storage losses, including through operating 
procedures, preventive maintenance, quality controls and inventory management practices, there can be no 
assurance that such measures will always be adequate to prevent or mitigate spillage, contamination, 
deterioration or other forms of product loss. In addition, the actual quantum of losses may vary depending on the 
volume handled, storage duration, weather conditions, equipment performance and other factors. Any material 
increase in spillage, handling losses, deterioration or product wastage, or any resulting operational disruption, 
environmental liability, customer claim or additional expenditure, could adversely affect our margins and 
inventory levels and consequently have a material adverse effect on our business, financial condition, results of 
operations and cash flows.

to new compliance requirements, including requiring us to obtain approvals and licenses from the Government

effective, each as of November 21, 2025. While we have not yet fully assessed the impact that these or similar

Security, 2020 is designed to standardise social security benefits for employees, which were previously divided 
under various acts with differing coverage. Additionally, the Code on Wages, 2019 restricts the portion of wages 
that can be excluded from the calculation of employee benefits (such as gratuity and maternity benefits) to a 
maximum of 50% of the total wages paid to employees. The implementation of such laws can increase our 
employee and labour costs and compliance related costs thereby adversely impacting our results of operations,

on the basis of the Red Herring Prospectus, the Bid cum Application Forms and the Revision Forms within the 
Price Band and the minimum Bid Lot. The Price Band and the minimum Bid lot will be decided by our 
Company, in consultation with the BRLMs, and if not disclosed in the Red Herring Prospectus, will be 
advertised in all editions of [●] (a widely circulated English national daily newspaper), all editions of [●] (a 
widely circulated Hindi national daily newspaper) and [●] editions of [●], a widely circulated Marathi regional 
daily newspaper, Marathi being the regional language of Maharashtra, India, where our Registered and

available to the Stock Exchanges for the purposes of uploading on their respective websites. The Offer Price 
shall be determined by our Company pursuant to the Book Building Process, in consultation with the BRLMs, 
after the Bid/ Offer Closing Date, in accordance with applicable law. See section titled “Offer Procedure” 
beginning on page 508. 
 
All Bidders, other than Anchor Investors, shall only participate in this Offer mandatorily through the 
ASBA process by providing the details of their respective ASBA Account in which the corresponding Bid

corresponding Bid Amount will be blocked by the SCSBs; or (ii) using the UPI Mechanism.Anchor 
Investors are not permitted to participate in the Offer through the ASBA process.  
 
In accordance with the SEBI ICDR Regulations, QIBs and Non-Institutional Bidders are not allowed to 
withdraw or lower the size of their Bids (in terms of the quantity of the Equity Shares or the Bid Amount) 
at any stage. Retail Individual Bidders (subject to the Bid Amount being up to ₹ 0.20 million) and Eligible 
Employees Bidding in the Employee Reservation Portion can revise their Bids during the Bid/ Offer 
Period and can withdraw their Bids on or before the Bid/ Offer Closing Date. Further, Anchor Investors 
cannot withdraw Bids after the Anchor Investor Bid/ Offer Period. Further, allocation to QIBs in the Net 
QIB Portion will be on a proportionate basis while allocation to Anchor Investors in the Anchor Investor 
Portion will be on a discretionary basis. Additionally, allotment to each Non-Institutional Bidder shall not 
be less than the minimum application size, subject to the availability of Equity Shares in the Non -
Institutional Portion, and the remaining Equity Shares, if any, shall be allotted on a proportionate basis.

Details of Equity Shares locked-in for six months  
 
In terms of Regulation 17 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, except for: 
 
1. the Minimum Promoters’ Contribution and any Equity Shares held by our Promoters in excess of the 
Minimum Promoters’ Contribution, which shall be locked in as above; 
2. any Equity Shares allotted to employees, whether currently an employee or not, pursuant to any 
employee stock option schemes, if any, prior to the Offer; 
3. Equity Shares held by an employee stock option trust or transferred to the employees by an employee 
stock option trust pursuant to exercise of options by the employees, whether currently employees or 
not, in accordance with the employee stock option plan or employee stock purchase scheme; 
4. Equity Shares held by a VCF or Category I AIF or Category II AIF or FVCI; 
5. Equity Shares offered pursuant to the Offer for Sale. 
 
the entire pre-Offer Equity Share capital held by persons other than our Promoters, will be locked-in for a period 
of six (6) months from the date of Allotment. In the event where lock-in of such pre-Offer Equity Share capital 
of our Company cannot be created, the relevant Depositories, upon instructions from our Company, shall record 
such Equity Shares as ‘non-transferable’ for such duration of six months from the date of Allotment in the 
Offer, in terms of Regulation 17(2) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations. 
 
In terms of Regulation 17(c) of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, Equity Shares held by a VCF or Category I AIF or 
Category II AIF or FVCI shall not be locked-in for a period of six (6) months from the date of Allotment, 
provided that such Equity Shares shall be locked in for a period of at least six (6) months from the date of 
purchase by such shareholders. 
 
Lock-in of Equity Shares Allotted to Anchor Investors 
 
50.00% of the Equity Shares Allotted to Anchor Investors in the Anchor Investors Portion shall be locked-in for 
a period of 90 days from the date of Allotment and the remaining 50.00% of the Equity Shares shall be locked-
in for a period of 30 days from the date of Allotment. 
 
Other Requirements in respect of Lock-in 
 
As required under Regulation 20 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, our Company shall ensure that the details of 
the Equity Shares locked-in are recorded by the relevant Depository. 
 
In terms of Regulation 21 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, the Equity Shares held by our Promoters which are 
locked-in as per Regulation 16 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations: (a) as Promoters’ Contribution, may be pledged 
only with scheduled commercial banks or public financial institutions or systemically important non-banking 
finance companies or deposit taking housing finance companies as collateral security for loans granted by such 
entity, provided that such loan has been granted for the purpose of financing one or more of the objects of the

133 
Offer, and pledge of the Equity Shares is one of the terms of the sanctioned loan; and (b) in excess of the 
Promoters’ Contribution, may be pledged only with scheduled commercial banks or public financial institutions 
or systemically important non-banking finance companies or deposit taking housing finance companies as 
collateral security for loans granted by such entity, provided that pledge of the Equity Shares is one of the terms 
of the sanctioned loan. However, such lock-in will continue pursuant to any invocation of the pledge and the 
transferee of the Equity Shares pursuant to such invocation shall not be eligible to transfer the Equity Shares 
until the expiry of the lock-in period stipulated above. 
 
In terms of Regulation 22 of the SEBI ICDR Regulations, Equity Shares held by our Promoters which are 
locked-in, may be transferred to Promoters or members of the Promoter Group or to any new promoter, subject 
to continuation of lock-in in the hands of the transferees for the remaining period and compliance with 
provisions of the Takeover Regulations, as applicable. The Equity Shares held by persons other than our 
Promoters and locked-in for a period of six months from the date of Allotment in the Offer or any other period 
as may be prescribed under applicable law, may be transferred to any other person holding Equity Shares which 
are locked-in, subject to the continuation of the lock-in the hands of the transferee for the remaining period and 
compliance with the provisions of the Takeover Regulations, as applicable.

Details of the Objects of the Fresh Issue 
 
1. Financing the modernisation and upgradation of Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility of our Company 
 
In accordance with our growth plans we plan to modernise and upgrade our Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility 
to increase the operational efficiency. Our Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility is situated at S. No. 7/1/A 8/1, Hol 
Tarfe Haveli, Bypass Road, Nandurbar, Maharashtra, 425412 and commenced operations in 1995. Our 
Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility, having solvent extraction plant, is involved in the production of feed grade 
soya meal with an approx protein content of 46% and has an installed capacity of 400 MTPD in each of Fiscals 
2026, 2025 and 2024, with an actual capacity utilization of 62.09%, 52.72% and 60.39%, respectively. For 
details in relation to our Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility, including in respect of its installed capacity and 
capacity utilization, see “Our Business – Capacity utilisation of our Manufacturing Facilities” on page 436. 
The machinery and equipment at our Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility are subjected to routine maintenance 
and periodic inspections to ensure uninterrupted operations, maintain efficiency, and minimize downtime. In 
addition to scheduled upkeep, we continue to allocate resources towards the procurement of new machinery and 
equipment. Such investments are undertaken not only to support our ongoing business activities but also to 
address the evolving operational needs and anticipated future requirements as assessed by our management, 
thereby enabling us to enhance productivity, improve operational reliability, and maintain long-term 
sustainability of our manufacturing processes. Further, one of our growth strategy is to capitalise on growth 
opportunities by enhancing our manufacturing capacities to cater the increasing demand of our products, as 
detailed in the section titled “Our Business – Our Strategies – Enhancing our Manufacturing Facilities to 
achieve improved economies of scale and facilitate the production of our ancillary and new products” on 
page 270. 
 
The proposed modernisation and upgradation of plant and machinery and civil works at our Nandurbar 
Manufacturing Facility is necessitated by the fact that the unit currently operates with ageing equipment, which 
limits the operational efficiency and product quality. Modernisation and upgradation of the facility will allow us 
to use advanced technology to improve quality, remain competitive, and meet changing market needs. Feed 
grade soya meal with approx 50% protein, which will be produced following the proposed modernization and 
upgradation is expected to offer higher margins compared to the conventional feed grade soya meal with approx. 
46% protein which is being produced at present. The ability to produce higher-protein soya meal is expected to 
enable the Company to cater to premium market segments and improve the overall product mix. The 
modernization will also help reduce downtime, contributing to improved operational efficiency and net quantity 
of product mix. This investment is indispensable for enhancing profitability and sustaining long-term growth.

142 
Ajay Girdharilal Chandak, Independent Chartered Engineer (“ICE”) vide his certificate dated September 08, 
2026 certifies that the proposed capital expenditure will lead to extensive revamp of our Nandurbar 
Manufacturing Facility so as to retain the existing 400 MTPD solvent extraction capacity while enabling 
additional production of soya meal with approx 50% protein content with improved efficiency and product 
quality. 
 
In this regard, we aim to utilize an aggregate of ₹ 138.44 million from the Net Proceeds towards Proposed 
Nandurbar Modernisation, thereby enhancing our operational efficiency, products quality and minimize 
downtime. The fund requirements, deployment schedule and the intended use of the Net Proceeds, for 
procurement of plant and machinery at our Nandurbar Manufacturing Facility, as described hereinabove, are 
based on our current estimates. The specific number and nature of such plant and machinery to be procured by 
our Company will depend on our business requirements. Accordingly, the details of our plant and machinery to 
be procured from the Net Proceeds will be suitably updated at the time of filing of the Red Herring Prospectus 
with the RoC. The modernisation for the aforesaid benefits has been approved by the Board of Directors of our 
Company pursuant to their resolution dated September 13, 2026. 
 
Our Company has obtained quotations and cost estimates from certain vendors for undertaking civil and 
building works, purchase and installation of plant and machinery and utilities, for the Proposed Nandurbar 
Modernisation. As of the date of this Draft Red Herring Prospectus, our Company is yet to place any orders or 
enter into definitive agreements or any memorandum of understanding for purchase and installation of majority 
of the new plant and machinery and implementation of building works and civil construction connected with

Utilities 
 
The proposed modernization is expected to be supported through the existing electrical infrastructure at the 
manufacturing facility, along with the proposed strengthening/upgradation of electrical systems wherever 
required. Water will be provided by borewells in the factory premises and power will be provided by 
Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Corporation Limited. 
 
2. Financing capital expenditure requirements at Dhule Manufacturing Facility of our Company 
towards (i) capacity enhancement and upgradation of refinery; and (ii) financing the setting up of 
packaging unit 
 
(i) 
Capacity enhancement and upgradation of refinery 
 
In accordance with our business strategies and growth plans we plan to enhance our refining capacity with 
addition of and upgradation our refinery at our Dhule Manufacturing Facility for increasing the refining capacity 
by 100 MTPD. 
 
Our Dhule Manufacturing Facility is situated at E-140 and E-140/1, MIDC, Awdhan, Dhule, Maharashtra, 
424311 and commenced operations in 1999. Dhule Manufacturing Facility is currently engaged in the 
production of edible refined oil and food grade soya meal protein products and the installed combined annual 
crude oil refining capacity was 61,050 MT for Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024 each, which recorded capacity 
utilization of 74.01%, 72.40% and 64.51%, respectively. For details in relation to the Dhule Manufacturing 
Facility, including in respect of its capacity and capacity utilization see “Our Business Capacity utilisation of 
our Manufacturing Facilities” on page 436.  
 
The machinery and equipment at our Dhule Manufacturing Facility are subjected to routine maintenance and 
periodic inspections to ensure uninterrupted operations, maintain efficiency, and minimize downtime. In 
addition to scheduled upkeep, we continue to allocate resources towards the procurement of new machinery and 
equipment. Such investments are undertaken not only to support our ongoing business activities but also to 
address the evolving operational needs and anticipated future requirements as assessed by our management, 
thereby enabling us to enhance productivity, improve operational reliability, and maintain long-term 
sustainability of our manufacturing processes. Further, one of our growth strategies is capitalising on growth 
enhancing our manufacturing capacities to cater the increasing demand of our products, as detailed in “Our 
Business – Our Strategies – Enhancing our Manufacturing Facilities to achieve improved economies of scale 
and facilitate the production of our ancillary and new products” on page 270. 
 
The Proposed Dhule Refinery Upgradation aims to increase our refining capacity from 150 MTPD to 250 
MTPD. This increase in our refining capacity will enable us to refine additional crude oil into refined oil which 
caters to growing consumer demand of ‘Murli’ brand edible oil and strengthens our market presence/ 
dominance. In addition to the proposed capacity enhancement, we plan to upgrade our refinery with installation

150 
of 50 tons dewaxing machine which will enable us to refine sunflower crude oil at our Dhule Manufacturing 
Unit.  
 
Overall, it will enhance operational efficiency, product mix, and long-term revenue growth. This we believe will 
result us to meet increasing demand of our existing and new customers. As certified by Ajay Girdharilal 
Chandak, Independent Chartered Engineer (“ICE”) vide their certificate dated September 08, 2026, the 
proposed capital expenditure will lead to increase in the refining capacity of our Dhule Manufacturing Facility 
from 150 MTPD to 250 MTPD after proposed capacity enhancement. 
 
In this regard, we aim to utilize an aggregate of ₹ 347.96 million from the Net Proceeds towards financing the 
Proposed Refinery Upgradation at our Dhule Manufacturing Facility, thereby enhancing our operational 
efficiency, refining capacity and product quality of our products. The fund requirements, deployment schedule 
and the intended use of the Net Proceeds, for the Proposed Refinery Upgradation at our Dhule Manufacturing 
Facility, as described hereinabove, are based on our current estimates. The specific number and nature of such 
plant and machinery to be procured by our Company will depend on our business requirements. Accordingly, 
the details of our plant and machinery to be procured from the Net Proceeds will be suitably updated at the time 
of filing of the Red Herring Prospectus with the RoC. The capacity enhancement and upgradation for the 
aforesaid benefits have been approved by the Board of Directors of our Company pursuant to their resolution 
dated September 13, 2026.  
 
Our Company has obtained quotations and cost estimates from certain vendors for the purchase and installation 
of plant and machinery, for the Proposed Refinery Upgradation. However, our Company is yet to place any 
orders or enter into definitive agreements or any memorandum of understanding for purchase and installation of 
majority of the new plant and machinery and implementation of building works and civil construction connected 
with the Proposed Refinery Upgradation.

Financing the setting up of Packaging Unit 
 
In line with our business strategies and growth plans, we intend to establish the Proposed Packaging Unit at our 
Dhule Manufacturing Facility to enhance both packaging capacity and efficiency. As of March 31, 2026, our 
existing packaging unit situated at Dhule Manufacturing Facility currently has a packaging capacity of 175 
MT/day. During the Fiscals 2026, 2025, and 2024, we packed/produced 58,460.09 MT, 51,240.70 MT, and 
50,045.98 MT of finished packed products, respectively. For details in relation to the packaging unit at Dhule 
Manufacturing Facility, including in respect of its packaging capacity and storage see section titled “Our 
Business – Capacity utilisation of our Manufacturing Facilities” on page 436. Further, one of our growth 
strategies is to capitalise on growth opportunities by enhancing our packaging quality and capacity to cater the

154 
increasing demand of our products, as detailed in “Our Business – Our Strategies - Enhancing our 
Manufacturing Facilities to achieve improved economies of scale and facilitate the production of our 
ancillary and new products” on page 270. 
 
The Proposed Packaging Unit alongwith warehouse adjacent to our Dhule Manufacturing Facility of 
approximately 11,200mt2 will increase capacity by 200 MT/day, taking total packaging capacity to 375 MT/day. 
This expansion is essential to align with the Proposed Refinery Upgradation to meet the growing demand for our 
packaged refined oil under the ‘Murli’ brand. It will enable efficient handling of a wide range of SKUs across 
all three refined oils in various pack sizes. The new 11,200.00 square meter facility is intended to support our 
growing operation needs which will be utilised for enabling organised inventory management and storage of 
night production. Overall, it will also improve packaging efficiency, inventory management, and product 
readiness for market distribution, particularly in view of the demand in the market, thereby increasing 
production efficiency and capacity ensuring optimum capacity utilisation for meeting the demand of our existing 
and new customers. As certified by Ajay Girdharilal Chandak, Independent Chartered Engineer (“ICE”) vide 
their certificate dated September 08, 2026, the proposed capital expenditure will lead to increase in the 
packaging capacity of our Dhule Manufacturing Facility from 175 MTPD in Fiscal 2026 to 375 MTPD after 
proposed capacity enhancement. 
 
In this regard, we aim to utilize an aggregate of ₹ 592.06 million from the Net Proceeds towards financing the 
Proposed Packaging Unit at our Dhule Manufacturing Facility thereby leveraging our packaging capacity for 
our products. The fund requirements, the deployment schedule and the intended use of the Net Proceeds, for 
procurement of equipment and machinery for the Proposed Packaging Unit at our Dhule Manufacturing Facility, 
as described hereinabove, are based on our current estimates. The specific number and nature of such equipment 
and machinery to be procured by our Company will depend on our business requirements. Accordingly, the 
details of our equipment and machinery to be procured from the Net Proceeds will be suitably updated at the 
time of filing of the Red Herring Prospectus with the RoC. The setting up of the Proposed Packaging Unit for 
the aforesaid benefits have been approved by the Board of Directors of our Company pursuant to their resolution 
dated September 13, 2026.  
 
Our Company has obtained quotations and cost estimates from certain vendors for the purchase and installation 
of equipment and machinery and utilities, for the establishment of new packaging unit. Further, our Company 
has placed work orders for the implementation of building works and civil construction connected with the 
Proposed Packaging Unit. However, our Company is yet to place any orders or enter into definitive agreements 
or any memorandum of understanding for purchase and installation of majority of the new equipment, 
machinery and utilities required for the Proposed Packaging Unit.

3. Financing the capacity enhancement, modernisation and upgradation of Gangakhed Manufacturing 
Facility of our Company 
 
In accordance with our growth plans we plan to modernise and upgrade our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility 
to increase the operational efficiency and product portfolio. Our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility is situated at 
P. No. B-7 & B-7/2, Kodri Road, Gangakhed MIDC, Margalwadi, Gangakhed, Parbhani, Maharashtra, 431514 
and our Company has acquired the said manufacturing facility in 2014. Our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility 
having solvent extraction plant, is involved in the production of soya crude oil and soya meal with a protein 
content of 46% and 50% and has a solvent extraction plant with an installed capacity of 500 MTPD in each of 
Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, with an actual capacity utilization of 59.38%, 58.42% and 59.70%, respectively. 
For details in relation to our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility, including in respect of its installed capacity and 
capacity utilization, see “Our Business – Capacity utilisation of our Manufacturing Facilities” on page 436. 
The machinery and equipment at our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility are subjected to routine maintenance 
and periodic inspections to ensure uninterrupted operations, maintain efficiency, and minimize downtime. In 
addition to scheduled upkeep, we continue to allocate resources towards the procurement of new machinery and 
equipment. Such investments are undertaken not only to support our ongoing business activities but also to 
address the evolving operational needs and anticipated future requirements as assessed by our management, 
thereby enabling us to enhance productivity, improve operational reliability, and maintain long-term 
sustainability of our manufacturing processes. Further, one of our growth strategy is to capitalise on growth 
opportunities by enhancing and scaling our manufacturing capacities to cater the increasing demand of our 
products, as detailed in the section titled “Our Business – Our Strategies – Enhancing our Manufacturing 
Facilities to achieve improved economies of scale and facilitate the production of our ancillary and new 
products” on page 270. 
 
The proposed capacity enhancement, modernisation and upgradation of plant and machinery at our Gangakhed 
Manufacturing Facility is necessitated by the fact that our Dhule Manufacturing Facility is operating at or near 
its existing capacity for production of food grade soya meal products, thereby limiting our ability to cater to 
incremental demand for such products. Accordingly, we intend to utilise the enhanced and currently 
underutilised capacities at our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility for production of food grade soya meal 
products, thereby enabling us to optimise capacity utilisation across our Manufacturing Facilities and cater to 
additional demand for such products. Modernisation and upgradation of the facility will allow us to diversify the 
product mix at our Gangakhed Manufacturing Facility from the existing production of conventional feed grade 
soya meal to higher-value food grade soya meal products, while improving our bottom line, operational 
efficiency, product quality and utilisation of the enhanced solvent extraction capacity. Soya meal food grade 
products which will be produced following the proposed modernization and upgradation is expected to offer 
higher margins compared to the conventional feed grade soya meal which is being produced at present. The 
modernization will also help reduce downtime, contributing to improved operational efficiency and net quantity 
of product mix. The proposed capacity enhancement will cover the preparatory section, solvent extraction plant 
and meal-processing section, along with associated electrical, utility and automation infrastructure. This 
investment is indispensable for enhancing profitability and sustaining long-term growth. Ajay Girdharilal 
Chandak, Independent Chartered Engineer (“ICE”) vide his certificate dated September 08, 2026 certifies that 
the proposed capital expenditure will lead to capacity enhancement, modernisation and upgradation of our

4. Funding the working capital requirements of our Company  
Our business is working capital intensive, primarily due to the seasonal nature of the agri-processing industry. 
During the peak periods, spanning the Kharif and Rabi seasons from October to March, we experience higher 
raw material supply and customer demand, necessitating larger inventories of both raw materials and finished 
goods. The primary component of our inventory is soyabean, which are procured in bulk to ensure uninterrupted 
production and timely order fulfillment. To support operations, we fund most of our working capital 
requirements through a combination of internal accruals and bank borrowings in the form of working capital 
facilities such as Cash Credit, Short Term Loans, and Pledge Loans. A substantial portion of this working 
capital is utilized for financing and replenishing inventory, while the balance is used to meet operational 
expenses and other current assets. 
At present, our operations are supported by 4 (four) silos and 4 (four) storage day bins capacity, which enable us 
to maintain approximately 83 days’ worth of soyabean inventory at our facilities. Given the support our current 
facilities provide, along with the modernization of Nandurbar and Gangakhed facilities and the upgrade of the 
Dhule refinery, expanding infrastructure is essential to manage higher demand and seasonal fluctuations. In line 
with our business expansion plans, we are in the process of erecting 2 (two) additional silos with a combined 
capacity of 24,800 MT. This will significantly enhance our ability to store larger volumes of both raw materials, 
ensuring smooth operations and responsiveness to market demand. Along with this, we are scaling up our oil 
refinery capacity by 100 TPD to strengthen production capabilities. As we undertake this expansion, our long-

166 
term working capital requirements are expected to rise, as we build larger inventories and scale operations at our 
existing facilities. 
We also manufacture a range of soya meal products across both food grade and feed grade categories, with 
varying protein contents to meet customer specifications. As these grades and protein specifications are not 
interchangeable, we are required to maintain separate finished goods inventories for each such variant, in 
addition to holding soyabean of the quality appropriate for their manufacture. This product mix requires us 
to carry a higher quantum of inventory over longer holding periods than a single-grade operation would 
entail, thereby further adding to our working capital requirements. 
In addition, we are increasing our presence in export markets, particularly for food-grade soya products. 
Our export sales are typically contracted on a forward basis with delivery schedules of four to six months, 
under which the sale price and the committed volumes are fixed at the time of entering into the contract. 
Since only approximately 50% to 55% of the soyabean seed is recovered as food-grade soya product, we 
require approximately 1.8x to 2.0x of soyabean for every contracted export volume. Consequently, in order 
to fulfil these committed export orders at pre-agreed prices, we are required to hedge our raw material 
exposure by procuring and holding soyabean inventory upfront, aligned to the delivery schedules under 
such contracts. This build-up of raw material inventory ahead of deliveries, over a procurement horizon 
longer than that of our domestic business, increases our long-term working capital requirements. 
Further, demand for our refined soyabean oil in consumer packs has been rising steadily. To service this 
demand, we propose to set up a new packing unit at Dhule and have expanded our product portfolio across 
multiple stock keeping units (“SKUs”) and pack sizes. The consumer pack business requires us to carry higher 
levels of finished goods inventory across each SKU, along with packaging material, and to extend credit to 
distributors and modern trade channels, each of which is expected to result in a substantial increase in our 
working capital requirements as this segment scales. 
We believe that the additional long-term working capital being sought is crucial to sustain uninterrupted 
operations, timely raw material procurement and efficient inventory management during peak seasons. This will 
not only support our growing production capacity but also enable us to meet customer demand consistently and 
strengthen our market position. 
 
As on March 31, 2026, our outstanding borrowings from banks under working capital facilities stood at 
₹2,744.36 million. Looking ahead, we expect to require additional long-term working capital to bridge the 
working capital gaps projected for Fiscal 2027, 2028, and 2029. We expect that funding these incremental 
requirements will be instrumental in helping us achieve growth targets and improving operational resilience and 
supply chain efficiency as we scale our business.

I) Current Assets 
Inventories 
Our Company’s inventories primarily consist of soyabeans (raw material), soya meal, 
and edible oils (finished goods). The days of inventory holding have been computed 
based on our historical Restated Standalone Financial Information, which reflects 
seasonal demand patterns and operational requirements. For Fiscal 2027, 2028, and 
2029, our Company has assumed inventory holding levels of 103 days, 96 days, and 97 
days of cost of material consumed, respectively. These assumptions are consistent with 
historical inventory trends as well as considering the proposed expansion plans and our 
experience in managing inventory during peak and non-peak seasons. In Fiscal 2026, 
inventory holding reached up to 83 days, with a mean of 77 days over the last three 
fiscals. Accordingly, inventory levels for Fiscals 2027, 2028, and 2029 have been 
projected in line with past trends as well as considering the proposed expansion plans, , 
thereby ensuring alignment with anticipated production schedules and the expected 
customer demand. The projected holding levels factor in the additional soyabean 
inventory required to be carried against our forward export contracts for food-grade 
soya products, which have delivery schedules of four to 6 six months and require raw 
material to be procured and hedged upfront, as well as the higher finished goods 
inventory to be maintained across multiple SKUs of consumer packs. This further 
reflect the separate inventories required to be maintained for our food grade and feed 
grade soya meal products across varying protein contents, which are not 
interchangeable and accordingly entail longer holding periods.

8. 
Profit after tax (PAT) means restated profit / (loss) for the financial year as appearing in the Restated Financial

10. Earnings per share (EPS) equals profit for the year attributable to the shareholders of the company divided by the 
Weighted average number of Equity Shares outstanding during the year and giving effect to Bonus Issuance. Since 
there is no dilutive capital, Basic and Diluted EPS would be same. 
11. Total borrowings refer to the sum of Non-current borrowings and current borrowings as appearing in Restated 
Financial Information. 
12. Adjusted Net Debt to Adjusted Equity Ratio is calculated as total interest bearing loans and borrowings less cash and 
cash equivalents and bank balances other than cash and cash equivalents divided by total equity attributable to the 
owners of the Company, comprising equity share capital, convertible preference shares, if any and other equity, as 
reported in the Restated Statement of Assets and Liabilities, and excludes non-controlling interest. 
13. Interest coverage ratio is calculated by dividing EBIT by Finance Costs. EBIT, i.e, Earnings before Interest and Taxes, 
is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the period / year, plus finance costs and total taxes 
14. Return on Net Worth is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the period / year divided by average net worth. Net 
Worth is calculated as the aggregate value of the paid-up share capital and all reserves created out of the profits and 
securities premium account and debit or credit balance of profit and loss account and non-controlling interest, after 
deducting the aggregate value of the accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not 
written off, as per the restated statement of assets and liabilities, but does not include reserves created out of 
revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation. Average net worth is the sum of opening and 
closing balance of net worth for relevant fiscal divided by two. 
15. Return on capital employed (ROCE) is calculated as EBIT divided by closing capital employed for the period / fiscal 
year. Earnings before Interest and Taxes (EBIT) is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the period / fiscal year, plus 
finance costs and total taxes. Capital employed is the sum of total equity plus debt consisting of borrowings and lease 
liabilities plus deferred tax liabilities less deferred tax assets, as appearing in the Restated Financial Information. 
16. Trade receivables days are calculated as Average Trade receivables divided by Revenue from operations and 
multiplied by number of days in the fiscal year. Average trade receivables is the sum of opening and closing balance of 
trade receivables for relevant fiscal divided by two. 
17. Inventory days are calculated as Average Inventory divided by Revenue from operations and multiplied by number of 
days in the fiscal year. Average Inventory is the sum of opening and closing balance of Inventory for relevant fiscal 
divided by two. 
18. Working Capital days is the sum of Inventory days and Trade Receivables days subtracted by Trade Payables days. 
Trade payables days are calculated as Average Trade payables divided by Revenue from operations and multiplied by 
number of days in the fiscal year. Average trade payables is the sum of opening and closing balance of trade payables 
for relevant fiscal divided by two.

ANNEXURE A 
 
THE STATEMENT OF POSSIBLE SPECIAL TAX BENEFITS AVAILABLE TO MAHARASHTRA 
OIL EXTRACTIONS LIMITED (THE “COMPANY”) AND ITS SHAREHOLDERS 
PART I 
 
Outlined below are the special tax benefits available to Maharashtra Oil Extractions Limited (the “Company”) 
and its shareholders under the Income Tax Act, 2025 (the “ITA”) and Income Tax Rules, 2026 (“Income Tax 
Rules”), circulars, notifications, as amended by the Finance Act 2026 (collectively, hereinafter referred to as 
“Income Tax Laws”). The possible special tax benefits are subject to fulfilment of conditions prescribed under 
the relevant Income Tax Laws by the Company or its shareholders. 
 
A. Special tax benefits available to the Company under the ITA and Income Tax Rules 
 
I. Lower Corporate tax rate under Section 200 of the ITA 
 
As per Section 200 read with Section 205(1) of the 2025 Act, corresponding to Section 115BAA of the Income 
Tax Act, 1961 (the “1961 Act”), a domestic company has an option to pay income tax in respect of its total 
income at a concessional tax rate of 22% (plus surcharge of 10% and health and education cess of 4%) provided 
the company does not avail of specified exemptions/ incentives/ deductions or set-off of specified losses/ 
unabsorbed depreciation etc., in the prescribed manner and complies with the other conditions specified in 
Section 200 read with Section 205(1) of the 2025 Act. In case a company opts for Section 200 of the 2025 Act, 
the provisions of Minimum Alternate Tax (“MAT”) under Section 206 of the 2025 Act, corresponding Section 
115JB of the 1961 Act, would not be applicable. The option needs to be exercised in the prescribed manner on 
or before the due date of filing the income tax return. The option once exercised cannot be subsequently 
withdrawn for the same or any other tax year and therefore, shall apply to subsequent tax years. Further, if the 
conditions mentioned in Section 200 read with Section 205(1) of the 2025 Act are not satisfied in any tax years, 
the option exercised shall become invalid in respect of such and subsequent tax years, and the other provisions 
of the 2025 Act shall apply as if the option under Section 200 of the 2025 Act had not been exercised. 
 
We understand that the Company intends to opt for the lower tax regime under 115BAA of 1961 Act for the tax 
return to be filed for financial year 2025-26. Accordingly, for tax year 2026-27, the Company shall be governed 
by the corresponding provisions of Section 200 read with Section 205(1) of the 2025 Act. Accordingly, MAT 
provisions under Section 206 of the 2025 Act will not be applicable to the Company. Further, any accumulated 
MAT credit from earlier years would not be available for set-off, as the benefit for utilisation of MAT credit is 
available only to companies opting for the lower tax regime on or after 1 April 2026. 
 
The provisions do not specify any limitation/condition on account of turnover, nature of business or date of 
incorporation for opting for the concessional tax rate. Accordingly, all existing as well as new domestic 
companies are eligible to avail this concessional rate of tax. 
 
Further the company’s subsidiary has availed the benefit of Section 201 of the 2025 Act which corresponds with 
section 115BAB of Income Tax Act 1961 the which provides concessional tax regime for new domestic 
manufacturing company subject to certain conditions being met and would be taxed at a concessional rate of 
15 % (plus applicable surcharge and cess). 
 
II. Deduction in respect of certain inter-corporate dividends under Section 148 of the ITA 
 
As per the provisions of Section 148 of the ITA, a domestic company shall be allowed to claim a deduction of 
dividend income earned from any other domestic company or a foreign company or a business trust. The 
amount of deduction so claimed should not exceed the amount of dividend distributed by it on or before the due 
date. In this case, due date means one month prior to the due date of furnishing return of income under sub-
section (1) of section 263 of the ITA. 
 
The Company has one subsidiary and thus, the Company should be eligible to claim deduction under section 
148 of the ITA in respect of dividends received (if any) from its subsidiary and further distributed to its 
shareholders subject to fulfilment of other conditions. The deduction under Section 148 is available even if a 
domestic company opts for concessional tax rate under Section 200 of ITA. 
 
The Company has not received any dividend in FY 2023-24, FY 2024-25 and FY 2025-26. Accordingly, no

191 
deduction under section 80M of ITA for the AY 2024-25, AY 2025-26 and AY 2026-27 was claimed by the 
Company. 
B. Special Tax Benefits available to the shareholders of the Company 
 
There are no special tax benefits available to the shareholders of the Company for investing in the equity shares 
of the Company. However, a shareholder shall be liable to concessional tax rates on certain incomes under the 
provisions of ITA. Further, it may be noted that these are general tax benefits available to equity shareholders, 
other shareholders holding any other type of instrument are not covered below. 
 
I. Dividend Income 
 
Dividend income earned by the shareholders would be taxable in their hands at the applicable rates. However, in 
case of shareholders who are individuals, Hindu undivided family, association of persons, body of individuals, 
whether incorporated or not and every artificial juridical person, maximum rate of surcharge would be restricted 
to 15%, irrespective of the amount of dividend. Further in case shareholder is a domestic company, deduction 
under Section 80M of the ITA would be available on fulfilling the conditions as mentioned above. Further, if the 
shareholder is a tax resident of a foreign country, dividend is taxable in India at a flat rate of 20% plus 
applicable surcharge and cess, subject to benefits available to residents of countries with which India has a 
Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (“DTAA”), it may claim benefit of applicable rate as stated in the 
DTAA, if more beneficial over rate in ITA. 
 
II. Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement Benefit

1.2.5 Trends in Household and Gross Savings 
 
Household savings are of the household sector, measured as the excess of income over consumption and 
invested in financial assets and physical assets. Household savings in India have grown at an 8.78% CAGR 
since FY18, reaching Rs 54.6 trillion in FY24, a 9.0% Y-o-Y increase. A shift toward physical assets, 
particularly housing and gold/silver ornaments, reflects a preference for tangible investments amid high inflation 
and slow growth in monetary assets. Savings in the form of gold and silver ornaments (% of Household sector 
savings) were reported at 1.2% in FY24.   
This increasing trend towards physical assets is occurring alongside a rise in household leverage, with 
borrowing, especially for housing, automobiles, and personal consumption, pushing household financial 
liabilities to a six-year high. Mutual funds and life insurance also grew, with an 11.5% and 13.6% Y-o-Y 
increase, respectively, while investment in equities and capital market instruments rose as they offer higher 
returns than bank deposits.

1.2.6 Growth of the middle class in India and the rural economy in India 
 
In FY25, FMCG growth slowed compared to the previous year, with rural areas showing signs of recovery 
towards the end of the year, especially in the last quarter, while urban demand stayed relatively subdued. The 
Reserve Bank of India (RBI) highlights that rising incomes and improved infrastructure are fueling increased 
rural consumption of FMCG products. This boost is supported by a rise in rural savings, marked by growing 
numbers of bank accounts and balances savings, and a reduction in inflationary pressures, which has allowed 
rural consumption to catch up with urban areas. Additionally, favorable monsoon conditions and improved 
sowing data are expected to sustain this growth, complemented by increased government spending on rural 
development and infrastructure. 
 
The expansion of middle-income households in rural India is transforming the country's economic landscape. 
This growth is driven by rising incomes, increased discretionary spending, a shift towards online and 
omnichannel shopping, and advancements in payment and logistics infrastructure. There is also a notable dietary 
shift in rural areas from carb-based foods to more protein-rich diets. India’s middle class, characterized by 
significant income variability, exhibits diverse spending patterns. Lower-middle-class households allocate much 
of their income to private healthcare, education, and essential consumer goods, such as motorbikes and basic 
appliances. In contrast, the upper-middle-class invests in luxury items, entertainment, property, and personal 
services, with a higher propensity to own assets like cars, computers, and air conditioners. Both segments of the 
middle class are substantial and emerging as key drivers of consumption and economic growth in India. Recent 
policies, including the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act, have increased rural 
incomes, enabling more rural households to enter the middle class. The growing, more inclusive, and politically 
engaged middle class reflects broader economic growth, although there is a risk of social strain if growth falters 
and quality job creation does not keep pace. 
 
The IMD’s forecast of a below-average southwest monsoon may adversely affect kharif production and limit 
reservoir replenishment, creating a near-term risk for rural incomes and consumption. Nevertheless, 
improvements in agricultural activity and rural spending remain important potential demand supports. The 
Government’s Budget measures focused on agriculture, infrastructure and rural development aim to raise 
incomes and revitalise the rural economy. These include agricultural research, new crop varieties, natural 
farming and stronger digital agricultural infrastructure. Effective implementation and timely fund allocation will 
be critical to improving farm incomes and supply chains. Over the longer term, a shift towards diversified, high-
value agriculture, supported by marketing and trade reforms, can foster more inclusive, environmentally 
sustainable and climate-resilient growth. Kharif crops are generally sown with the onset of the southwest 
monsoon (June–July) and harvested around September–October, while rabi crops are sown in October–

199 
November and harvested in spring (March–April). Major kharif crops include paddy, maize and cotton; major 
rabi crops include wheat, mustard and gram. 
 
Despite higher absolute incomes among the wealthy, the sheer size of India's middle class indicates it will 
become a major force in the economy, creating one of the world's largest markets. This burgeoning middle class, 
with its growing discretionary spending power, is poised to drive investment, generate employment, and spur 
further economic growth. Assuming effective reforms are implemented, and the middle class expands to over 
one billion people, its role will be pivotal in India's economic and social fabric, influencing a wide range of 
activities from consumption to employment and political change.
