1.2.8 Concluding Remarks 
 
From a macroeconomic standpoint, India remains one of the most resilient large economies in a challenging 
global environment. The IMF forecasts GDP growth for India at 6.40% in CY26, far outpacing the estimated 
CY26 global average of 3.00%. This performance reflects a combination of strong domestic fundamentals, 
policy stability and a sustained focus on capital formation. While the global economy continues to face 
uncertainty from geopolitical conflicts, commodity price volatility and rising public debt, India’s diversified 
growth drivers, stable policy framework and expanding export ecosystem position it well to navigate these 
headwinds.

202 
The key sectors with potential exposure to changes in US tariff policy include engineering goods, electronics, 
gems and jewellery, pharmaceuticals, textiles and automobiles/auto components, given their material export 
linkages to the US market. 
 
As of August 2026, the US-India trade relationship faces renewed uncertainty. The US Senate has passed the 
Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which could allow the US President to impose tariffs of up to 
100% on goods from major buyers of Russian energy, including India. The bill is not itself a 100% tariff 
currently in force, but it creates a significant additional risk for Indian exporters if enacted and applied. In July 
2026, the US had imposed a baseline tariff of 10% on roughly 70% of Indian manufactured exported goods 
(covering textiles, engineering items, gems, and machinery. 
 
India continues to strengthen its position through diversification of trade partnerships and expansion of FTAs 
with the European Union, the United Kingdom, EFTA and other key economies. India continues to strengthen 
its position through diversification of trade partnerships and expansion of FTAs. The India-UK Free Trade 
Agreement officially came into effect on 15th July 2026, providing improved market access and lower trade 
barriers between the two countries. The agreement is expected to support greater trade in goods and services and 
create new opportunities for Indian exporters. India is also continuing engagement with the EU, EFTA, GCC 
and other key markets to reduce dependence on any single trading partner. 
 
The US-Iran conflict remains ongoing and uncertainties around the same remain. As of August 2026, 
negotiations have stalled, with the US stating that no formal talks are currently planned with Iran. The Iran 
conflict has led to an increase in prices of consumer products in India due to potentially higher fuel, freight and 
input costs, which can make everyday goods like FMCG items, plastics and packaged foods more expensive. 
Disruptions in shipping and fertiliser supplies are also pushing up food prices, affecting imports of agricultural 
inputs and leading to costlier food products for consumers. Overall, delays in trade routes and rising logistics 
costs are reducing availability and increasing prices of imported consumer goods, especially from Gulf-linked 
supply chains. Overall, this is leading to supply shortages, rising costs, and production slowdowns in India’s 
chemical and pharma sectors, with the impact likely to worsen if the conflict continues. Prolonged geopolitical 
tensions or conflict in the region could lead to sustained increases in crude oil and LPG prices, which may 
translate into higher input costs across industries and contribute to inflationary pressures in the Indian economy. 
 
The National Mission on Edible Oils – Oilseeds (NMEO-OS), approved for the FY2024-25 to FY2030-31 
period, further strengthens the policy focus on agricultural productivity, rural incomes and import resilience. 
With a total outlay of Rs. 10,103.38 crore comprising Rs. 7,481.67 crore from the Centre and Rs. 2,621.71 crore 
from States- the mission targets an increase in primary oilseed production from 39 million tonnes to 69.7 million 
tonnes by 2030–31. It focuses on key crops including rapeseed-mustard, soybean, groundnut, sunflower and 
sesamum, while also promoting secondary sources such as cottonseed, rice bran and tree-borne oils. By 
improving seed availability, productivity, procurement, processing and value-chain linkages, the mission could 
support farm incomes, strengthen domestic edible-oil supply and reduce import dependence over the medium 
term. 
 
Domestically, a below-normal monsoon and potential El Niño conditions may contribute to higher food 
inflation, which could affect household spending and consumer sentiment, particularly in rural markets. 
Elevated prices of essential commodities may reduce discretionary spending; however, strong domestic demand, 
urban consumption, and rising income levels are expected to support overall growth in the consumer sector. 
 
Policy momentum remains strong. The 56th meeting of the GST Council marked a major structural reform by 
proposing a simplified two-rate system of 5% and 18%, replacing the earlier four-slab framework, along with a 
40% demerit rate for luxury and sin goods. This rationalisation aims to reduce compliance burdens, enhance 
efficiency, and stimulate private consumption. Together with recent revisions in personal income tax rates, these 
measures are projected to release savings exceeding Rs 2.5 lakh crore into the economy, supporting demand and 
easing inflationary pressures. 
 
The Union Budget’s allocation of Rs 12.20 lakh crore for capital expenditure in FY27 further reinforces the 
government’s commitment to infrastructure-led growth. Public investment is expected to catalyse private sector 
activity, evidenced by rising project announcements and growing imports of capital goods. Rural demand and 
agricultural investment remain supported by policy measures, though a below-normal monsoon outlook and 
food-inflation risks may temper near-term consumption conditions.

2.1 Overview of the Structure of Edible Oil Market in India 
 
The Indian edible oil market was valued at Rs. 4,432 billion in FY26 and is projected to reach Rs. 5,400 billion 
by FY29, registering a CAGR of 8.1% during FY24–FY29. Market growth is being supported by rising per 
capita edible oil consumption, population growth, increasing urbanisation, changing dietary habits, and 
expanding demand from the food processing and HoReCa sectors. At the same time, government initiatives 
aimed at enhancing domestic oilseed production are expected to strengthen long-term supply security and 
reduce import dependence. 
 
India remains one of the world's largest producers of oilseeds as well as one of the largest consumers of edible 
oils. Globally, the edible oil sector has expanded significantly, driven largely by the production of soybean, 
palm, groundnut and rapeseed oils, alongside moderate growth in sunflower seed oil production. India ranks as 
the fourth-largest player in this global landscape, after the USA, China, and Brazil, contributing 
approximately 15–20% of the global oilseed area, 6–7% of total vegetable oil production, and 9–10% of global 
consumption. According to the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers' Welfare's 3rd Advance Estimates, the 
country is estimated to produce 42.61 million tonnes of oilseeds during the 2024-25 crop year. Despite this 
strong production base, domestic output continues to fall short of demand, resulting in imports accounting for 
nearly 57% of India's edible oil consumption. This high dependence on imports leads to an annual foreign 
exchange outflow of approximately USD 20.56 billion, prompting the Government of India to intensify efforts 
to improve self-sufficiency through higher domestic oilseed cultivation

Consumption patterns across India vary significantly by region. Groundnut oil continues to dominate in the 
western and southern states, while mustard and rapeseed oil are widely consumed in northern and eastern India. 
Coconut and sesame oils remain preferred in parts of southern India, whereas soybean, sunflower, palm, 
cottonseed and rice bran oils have gained widespread acceptance across the country owing to advancements in 
refining, bleaching and deodorisation technologies that have improved product quality and versatility. Palm oil 
continues to account for the largest share of edible oil imports, contributing nearly 59% of total imports, with 
refined palmolein witnessing strong demand from hotels, restaurants and food processing industries. While 
western India remains an important production and distribution hub, significant consumption of soybean, 
sunflower and mustard oils is concentrated in northern and central parts of Indian markets, highlighting the need 
for robust distribution networks across regions. 
 
To reduce import dependence, the Government of India launched the National Mission on Edible Oils – Oil 
Palm (NMEO-OP) in August 2021 with the objective of expanding oil palm and other oilseed cultivation and 
increasing domestic crude palm oil (CPO) production to 11.20 lakh tonnes by 2025-26, out of which the 
production has raised to 3.80 lakh tonnes in 2024-25.Covering 15 states and 21.75 lakh hectares, the mission 
provides farmers with quality planting material, assured buyback arrangements, and viability gap payments 
(VGPs) to protect them from fluctuations in international prices. The initiative forms a key pillar of India's 
broader strategy to achieve self-reliance in edible oils while improving farm incomes.

Further strengthening this vision, the Union Cabinet approved the National Mission on Edible Oils – Oilseeds 
(NMEO-Oilseeds) in October 2024 with targets extending to 2030-31. Together, NMEO-OP and NMEO-
Oilseeds aim to increase domestic edible oil production to 25.45 million tonnes, enabling India to meet nearly 
72% of its projected edible oil demand through domestic sources. The missions also target an increase in 
primary oilseed production from 39 million tonnes in 2022-23 to 69.7 million tonnes by 2030-31, reinforcing 
India's transition towards a more resilient, sustainable and self-reliant edible oil ecosystem. As of 2025-26 
oilseed production has increased to 43.06 million tonnes.

2.6 Product- Wise Import of Edible Oil 
 
The import duty structure for major edible oils has undergone considerable variation during FY20–FY26, 
reflecting India's efforts to balance consumer affordability, domestic oilseed producer interests, and import

moderating to 29.1% in FY26.

particularly notable, potentially improving the relative competitiveness of domestically produced soybean oil, 
while the lower duty on crude sunflower oil provides greater flexibility for meeting domestic supply gaps.

2.10 Movement in Prices of Edible Oil 
 
Edible oil prices witnessed significant volatility during FY19–FY26, primarily influenced by global commodity 
cycles, supply chain disruptions, weather-related production issues, and geopolitical developments. Prices across 
all major edible oils increased sharply between FY19 and FY22, reaching a cyclical peak in FY22. Rapeseed oil 
recorded the highest realization at USD 2,053/tonne, followed by Others (USD 1,942/tonne) and Sunflower oil 
(USD 1,938/tonne), reflecting tight global supplies and elevated input costs. Palm oil, despite remaining the 
lowest-priced edible oil throughout the period, also witnessed a substantial increase from USD 959/tonne in 
FY19 to USD 1,535/tonne in FY22, reinforcing its cost advantage over competing oils. 
 
Following the FY22 peak, prices moderated across all oil categories during FY23 and FY24 as global supply 
conditions improved and commodity markets normalized. However, a gradual recovery was observed in FY25 
and FY26, supported by weather-related production concerns in key producing regions and firm international 
demand. Despite these fluctuations, the relative price hierarchy remained largely unchanged, with palm oil 
consistently retaining the lowest realization, making it the preferred choice for price-sensitive consumers and 
industrial users, while rapeseed and specialty oils continued to command premium realizations due to 
comparatively higher production costs and limited availability. This persistent price differential continues to 
influence India's edible oil consumption mix and import sourcing strategy.

2.11 Government Support & Overview of Key Regulatory Factors impacting the Industry in India 
 
The edible oil sector in India is among the largest globally and is essential in satisfying the increasing need for 
cooking oils within the country. Nevertheless, India still heavily depends on imports to satisfy its demand for 
edible oil despite consuming a large amount. India is the largest importer of edible oils in the world. The 
government has taken initiative to tackle this issue by implementing different regulations and programs to 
decrease reliance on imports, control prices, and increase local oilseed production. 
 
Technology Mission on Oilseeds in 1986- This project focused on boosting the local oilseed production and 
attaining independence in edible oil production. In 2014, the government's dedication to encouraging oilseed 
cultivation led to the expansion of the mission to include the National Mission on Oilseeds and Oil Palm 
(NMOOP). 
 
Import Duty Adjustments- Effective September 14, 2024, the government raised the BCD on crude edible oils 
from 0% to 20%, bringing the total import duty to 27.5% (including AIDC and other charges). This revision was 
aimed at supporting domestic oilseed farmers by reducing the competitiveness of imported oils. However, as on 
June 11, 2025, the Centre reduced the BCD on crude sunflower, soybean, and palm oils from 20% to 10%, 
increasing the duty differential between crude and refined edible oils from 8.75% to 19.25%. This adjustment 
was intended to address the escalation in edible oil prices that followed the September 2024 hike and concurrent 
increases in international market prices. The widened duty differential encourages higher domestic refining 
capacity utilization and discourages imports of refined oils. Import duties remain a critical factor influencing the 
landed cost of edible oils and, in turn, domestic prices. By lowering the duty on crude oils, the government aims 
to reduce landed costs and retail prices, provide relief to consumers, cool overall inflation, and still ensure fair 
compensation for farmers. 
 
Technological and E-Governance Initiatives- The Department of Food and Public Distribution's Directorate 
of Sugar & Vegetable Oils created a web-based platform (evegoils.nic.in) for vegetable oil producers to submit 
data online monthly. This system allows the government to quickly make data-informed policy decisions by 
providing transparency. It also helps streamline the effective handling of monthly production data and 
registration of new edible oil facilities. 
 
As an example, businesses looking to set up new facilities for producing edible oils can now sign up through the 
National Single Window System (NSWS), making the process even more straightforward and promoting 
investment in the industry. 
 
Furthermore, overseeing prices and interfering in the retail pricing of edible oils also aids in guaranteeing 
affordability for consumers. Government meetings with industry stakeholders like the Solvent Extraction 
Association of India (SEAI) and Indian Vegetable Oil Producers' Association (IVPA) have played a crucial role 
in adjusting retail prices to match global market trends. 
 
Impact of Recent U.S. Tariffs- In August 2025, the United States doubled tariffs on several Indian exports, 
raising total duties up to 50%. Since India is a major importer of edible oils rather than an exporter, and the U.S. 
is not a significant supplier, there is no direct effect on edible oil trade. However, reduced export earnings from 
other sectors can pressure the rupee, raising the landed cost of edible oils that India imports largely from 
Indonesia, Malaysia, Argentina, Brazil, and Ukraine. Indirectly, tariff-driven trade shifts, especially in 
commodities like soybean oil, may also affect global pricing. These developments emphasize India’s 
dependence on imports and the importance of expanding domestic oilseed production to reduce vulnerability. 
 
2.12 Key Drivers & Risks for Edible Oil Industry in India 
 
One of the key factors behind the growth of India's edible oil sector is its significant level of consumption, 
which ranks it as one of the leading consumers of edible oil worldwide. The increase in demand for processed 
and packaged oils in households, food services, and industrial sectors is mostly attributed to population growth, 
higher incomes, and urbanization. Moreover, the increasing demand for healthier oils like olive and sunflower 
oil has fueled growth in various oil segments. Government programs, such as the National Mission on Edible 
Oils-Oil Palm (NMEO-OP), strive to decrease reliance on imports by increasing local oilseed production. These 
programs aid India in its effort to improve self-reliance, potentially reducing price fluctuations impacted by 
global markets.

215 
Further, the industry's growth is heavily influenced by technological breakthroughs and enhancements in the 
supply chain. The efficiency of production has been enhanced by the introduction of high-yield oilseed varieties, 
modern farming techniques, and oil refining technologies. Innovations in the supply chain, such as cold-pressed 
and organic oils, serve health-conscious consumers. Additionally, positive trade policies and incentives promote 
investment in oilseed processing and refining infrastructure, increasing India's ability to withstand global supply 
interruptions. The emphasis on boosting local capability, combined with a rise in structured retail outlets, 
prepares India's edible oil sector for continual expansion. 
 
Key Risks 
 
The Indian edible oil sector is exposed to numerous risks, particularly its significant reliance on imported goods. 
Approximately 55-60% of the need for edible oil is satisfied by imports, primarily from nations such as 
Indonesia, Malaysia, and Argentina. Relying on international markets makes the industry susceptible to 
fluctuations, such as shifts in global production, export limitations, and geopolitical tensions, which can cause 
sudden price changes and interruptions in supply. For instance, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine 
impacted the import of sunflower oil, highlighting the dangers associated with geopolitical events. Moreover, 
the fluctuating weather patterns caused by climate change also present threats to both local and worldwide 
oilseed cultivation, affecting the supply and costs of necessary cooking oils. 
 
Another important drawback involves the possible health and environmental issues linked to specific oils, like 
palm oil, which holds a significant market portion in India. Critics frequently condemn palm oil production in 
exporting countries for causing deforestation and environmental damage, leading to concerns about ethics and 
sustainability. Within the country, an increase in consumer knowledge and a transition towards more nutritious 
and environmentally friendly food options could lead to a decrease in the need for specific oils, impacting the 
market situation. Fluctuations in prices caused by inflation and changes in currency also contribute to these 
risks, impacting profit margins and creating difficulty for companies in keeping pricing and supply levels stable. 
To manage these risks, it is necessary to implement various sourcing tactics, encourage sustainable production 
methods, and find a balance between cost and quality to cater to the needs of a market that is sensitive to prices. 
 
2.13 Industry Growth Drivers & Outlook 
 
India's edible oil sector is well positioned for substantial expansion due to increasing population, urbanization, 
and changing eating patterns. Projections indicate that India's population will increase to 1.66 billion by CY47, 
up from 1.41 billion in CY21. The growth in population along with higher disposable incomes will result in an 
increasing need for edible oils, specifically for cooking and food processing. In 2022–23, India’s consumption 
stood at 28.92 million tons, while in 2023–24 it moderated slightly to 27.83 million tons. Domestic production 
continues to meet only around 40–45% of requirements, with imports bridging the gap in 2022–23 alone, India 
imported nearly 16.5 million tons of edible oils. According to NITI Aayog, under current trends, India’s 
domestic supply is projected to rise to 16 million tons by 2030 and 26.7 million tons by 2047. However, demand 
is expected to grow faster than supply. In one scenario where per capita consumption reaches the average of 
developed countries (25.3 kg), the demand–supply gap could be about 22.3 million tons by 2030 and 15.2 
million tons by 2047. In a higher consumption scenario comparable to U.S. levels (40.3 kg), the gap could 
widen to 29.5 million tons by 2030 and 40 million tons by 2047. The rise in demand will mainly be fueled by 
household consumption, underscoring the importance of sustainable oil production to satisfy the increasing 
demand.

Government programs like the National Mission on Oilseeds and Oil Palm (NMOOP) and the National Food 
Security Mission (NFSM) play a crucial role in shaping the industry's future. These efforts seek to increase the 
production of oilseeds within the country, lessen the nation's reliance on imports (currently at 55-60%), and 
maintain stable prices. The government is setting up the sector for long-term growth by upgrading infrastructure, 
offering seed technology, and giving incentives to oilseed farmers. 
 
Overall, the edible oil sector in India is predicted to experience consistent growth by reaching market size of 
INR 4,41,176 crores by CY28, propelled by factors such as population changes, rising incomes, and shifting 
dietary tastes. Government strategies will be crucial in securing the industry's future sustainability and 
decreasing reliance on imports.

3.5 Key Growth Drivers & Limiting Factors/ Challenges shaping the Global Soybean Processing Industry 
Growth Drivers 
• The global soybean processing industry is experiencing growth due to several core drivers. Increasing 
demand for plant-based proteins is a major factor, as consumers seek healthier and more sustainable protein 
options. Soy protein is widely used in foods ranging from meat substitutes to dairy alternatives, propelling 
demand in both developed and emerging markets. 
 
• The expansion of the animal feed market is another significant contributor, with soybean meal—a key by 
product—serving as a vital source of protein for livestock, poultry, and aquaculture. Rising global meat 
consumption, particularly in regions like Asia-Pacific where livestock farming is growing rapidly, is driving 
demand for soybean meals.  
 
• Growing biofuel use, especially in biodiesel, further supports industry growth. As countries push for 
renewable energy sources to meet carbon reduction goals, soybean oil is increasingly used as a biodiesel 
feedstock, particularly in North America and Europe, where biofuel mandates are in place. 
 
• Further, advances in soybean processing technology have improved extraction efficiency and product 
quality, helped companies’ lower costs and produce better-quality oils and meals. Innovations in crop 
genetics also enable higher yields, providing a larger supply of raw materials to meet rising demand. These 
combined factors are anticipated to sustain the soybean processing industry’s growth in the coming years. 
 
• Consumer demand for plant-based, sustainable, and healthy food options is also creating new growth 
avenues. Diversification into products like soy protein isolates or soy-based meat alternatives allows 
companies to tap into this expanding trend. Similarly, diversifying into biodiesel production or industrial 
applications of soy byproducts can help meet the increasing global demand for renewable energy and eco-
friendly materials. These combined factors are anticipated to sustain the soybean processing industry’s 
growth in the coming years. 
 
Challenges 
• The global soybean processing industry faces several key challenges impacting profitability and growth. 
Soybean prices and market demand can fluctuate based on weather conditions, global supply, and changes in

222 
consumer preferences. Commodity price volatility, driven by weather, crop yields, and fluctuating global 
demand, creates financial pressure as stable, affordable raw materials are critical for industry margins. 
Additionally, environmental and regulatory pressures have increased as soybean production is linked to 
deforestation and emissions, particularly in Brazil. Stricter regulations and rising consumer awareness 
demand more sustainable practices, adding to operational costs. 
 
• Supply chain disruptions add further strain, exposing vulnerabilities and raising transport costs. Trade 
tensions, especially between the U.S. and China, add market uncertainties. Moreover, competition from 
alternative plant-based proteins such as pea and hemp could impact soybean demand, as consumers explore 
diverse protein options with varied nutritional profiles. 
3.6 Trend of Average Annual Global Soya Bean Oil Prices 
 
Soya bean prices and market demand can fluctuate based on weather conditions, global supply, and changes in 
consumer preferences. Global soybean oil prices exhibited significant volatility during CY19–CY25, increasing 
from USD 645/tonne in CY19 to USD 1,385/tonne in CY25, representing more than a two-fold increase over 
the period. Prices remained relatively stable during CY19–CY20 before rising sharply to USD 1,277/tonne in 
CY21 and reaching a peak of USD 1,566/tonne in CY22, amid tighter global edible oil supplies, elevated 
commodity prices and supply-chain disruptions. Prices subsequently moderated to USD 1,273/tonne in CY23 as

CY25. Oil prices are expected to hover around USD 1500/tonne by CY26.

soybean availability, weather conditions in major producing regions, biofuel demand and broader edible oil 
market dynamics. The recovery during CY24–CY25 also indicates renewed firmness in the market following 
the CY23 correction. Given soybean oil's role as a major edible oil and its increasing use in food applications 
and biofuels, global prices are expected to remain sensitive to changes in soybean production, crushing margins, 
competing vegetable oil prices and energy markets.

4.5 Toasted & Untoasted Soybean Meal  
 
4.5.1 Overview 
 
India is a major producer of soybean meal, with Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan being key 
regions. Toasted soybean meal, known for its high protein content and digestibility, dominates the market as a 
primary component of animal feed. In contrast, untoasted soybean meal, rich in active enzymes, is used in 
specialized applications such as poultry feed and industrial products. Untoasted soybean meal, also known as 
full fat enzyme active soya flour, can be used as a food ingredient, particularly in bakery and food processing 
industries. Toasted and untoasted soy flakes and grits are suitable for use as a protein fortifying ingredient in 
many food manufacturing processes and exports for food applications. 
 
4.5.2 Market Size Trend  
 
The India toasted and untoasted soybean meal market has expanded from Rs 338 billion in FY19 to Rs 667 
billion in FY26, despite some volatility during FY20–FY22, reflecting fluctuations in soybean availability, 
processing volumes and soybean meal prices. The market is projected to reach Rs 792 billion by FY29, 
registering a 5.9% CAGR during FY26–FY29. The recovery from Rs 387 billion in FY21 to Rs 538 billion in 
FY23 and further to Rs 667 billion in FY26 highlights the market's sensitivity to soybean crop cycles and 
downstream feed demand. 
 
Going forward, demand is expected to remain supported by the expansion of India's poultry, dairy, livestock and 
aquaculture industries, where soybean meal is an important protein source. However, the relatively moderate 
projected CAGR indicates a more mature market, with growth likely to be driven primarily by underlying feed 
consumption rather than significant expansion in per-unit demand. Domestic soybean availability, crushing 
margins, soybean meal prices and export-import dynamics will remain key factors influencing market growth 
through FY29.

4.8 Key Trends and Growth Drivers of Indian Soybean Processing Industry 
 
The Indian soybean processing industry is set for substantial growth, driven by increasing consumer demand for 
nutritious food, sustainability efforts, and strategic international investments. Currently growing at a CAGR of 
12.2% over past six years from CY18 to CY24, the sector is well-positioned to help address the country's 
protein deficiency. The market is expected to grow at a CAGR of ~5% until CY28. By incorporating soybean 
processing into government nutrition programs, the industry can make soy-based products more accessible at the 
local and regional levels, offering affordable and nutritious options to a wider population while also creating job 
opportunities. 
 
Recent investments from countries like Japan and the Netherlands highlight the vast potential of the Indian soy 
food processing market. Although soy has not traditionally been a staple in Indian diets, rising awareness of its 
health benefits is boosting demand for high-quality processed soy products. Due to advanced processing 
techniques and innovations, Indian soy food companies have enhanced product quality significantly. This 
emphasis on quality allows the industry to meet the needs of health-conscious consumers who prioritize superior 
taste and nutrition. 
 
Further, the Indian soybean processing industry is driven by increasing domestic and global demand for 
soybean-derived products, particularly edible oil and animal feed. With India heavily reliant on edible oil 
imports, the government has been promoting oilseed cultivation through higher Minimum Support Prices (MSP) 
and incentives. The steady cultivation area of 118.32 lakh hectares, concentrated in Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, and Rajasthan, ensures a consistent supply of raw material. Additionally, advancements in 
processing technology and improved logistics have enhanced efficiency, making soybean processing more 
competitive.

industry growth, while measures to achieve self-sufficiency in edible oil production have provided 
further impetus. Additionally, import regulations and adjustments in duties on edible oils have been 
designed to protect domestic processors and farmers, thereby positively influencing market dynamics 
and ensuring stability. The Indian government has been promoting oilseed cultivation through higher 
Minimum Support Prices (MSP) and incentives and Bhavantar schemes. 
 
2. Export Opportunities: Export opportunities have also significantly contributed to the growth of the 
Indian soybean processing industry. Indian soymeal, toasted/ untoasted Flakes and grits and Soya 
Lecithin, known for being non-GMO, holds a competitive edge in international markets, driving 
demand and boosting export revenues. Strategic trade policies aimed at liberalizing trade have the 
potential to further enhance India’s access to global markets, providing additional avenues for 
expansion and revenue generation. 
 
3. Technological Advancements: Technological advancements have played a pivotal role in enhancing 
the efficiency and profitability of the soybean processing industry. The adoption of modern processing 
technologies has not only improved extraction rates but has also enhanced the overall quality of the 
end products. These advancements have enabled industry to diversify its product offerings, including 
the production of soy milk, tofu, soy sauce and textured vegetable protein, catering to the growing 
segment of health-conscious consumers and the rising popularity of plant-based diets.

consumption patterns are driving demand for soy-based foods such as soy milk, tofu, soy flour, and 
textured vegetable protein (TVP). Soy is increasingly being integrated into Indian diets due to its high 
nutritional value, affordability, and versatility in cooking. Improved taste and quality, driven by 
advancements in processing technologies, are helping soy-based products appeal to mainstream 
consumers.

infrastructure for the food processing sector, as evidence by the approval of 1134 food processing 
projects including 41 Mega Food Parks and 395 Cold chain projects across the country till June 2025.

developments enable the soybean processing industry to enhance its supply chain efficiency, reduce 
wastage, and improve product quality through better storage and distribution facilities.

based foods offer a cost-effective plant-based solution. Incorporating soy into government nutrition 
programs can improve accessibility and drive consumption at the grassroots level. Expansion in soy 
food usage can help achieve national food security goals while supporting rural livelihoods.

4.9 Key Risks and Challenges faced by the Soybean Processing Industry  
The Indian soybean processing industry faces risks from erratic monsoons and water scarcity, as key producing 
states rely on rain-fed irrigation. Fluctuating global prices and high import dependence add market volatility, 
impacting profitability. 
Rising input costs, storage and transport inefficiencies, and policy uncertainties further challenge the sector. 
Additionally, competition from GMO soybeans globally puts pressure on Indian producers. Improved irrigation, 
technology adoption, and policy support are key to mitigating these challenges. 
 
1. High Cost of Inputs: The high cost of inputs, including energy, labor, and raw materials, can 
significantly impact the operational margins of processing units. The industry relies on a variety of 
resources, and rising costs for these inputs can lead to decreased profitability, especially for smaller 
players who may not have the financial flexibility to absorb such increases. Additionally, the cost of 
adopting and maintaining advanced technology to enhance processing efficiency can be prohibitive for 
many processing units. 
2. Quality Control and Standardization Issues: Ensuring consistent quality in processed soybean 
products remains a challenge, particularly for smaller processing units. Quality variations often stem 
from inconsistent raw material supply and the absence of standardized processing protocols. While 
larger players have increasingly invested in modern equipment and quality control systems, many 
smaller units still face constraints in adopting advanced technology, leading to variability in product 
quality. This inconsistency can impact the competitiveness of Indian soybean products in domestic and 
export markets and may hinder the industry’s ability to fully meet the rising demand for high-quality 
soy-based products. 
3. Climate Dependence and Impact: One of the primary risks for the Indian soybean processing 
industry is its heavy dependence on weather conditions. Soybean cultivation is predominantly rain-fed, 
making it highly vulnerable to monsoon variability. Unpredictable rainfall patterns, droughts, or 
excessive rainfall can lead to reduced yields and inconsistent raw material supply, impacting 
processing operations and profitability. Climate change poses an additional risk, exacerbating these 
weather-related challenges and adding to the uncertainty of agricultural outputs. 
4. Volatility in Prices: The industry is exposed to significant price volatility in the global market. 
Fluctuations in international soybean prices, influenced by factors such as global production levels, 
trade policies, and geopolitical events, can directly affect the profitability of soybean processors. Price 
instability can make it difficult for processors to plan operations effectively and manage financial 
risks, impacting both large and small-scale processors. 
5. Environmental and Sustainability Concerns: Sustainability is becoming an increasingly important 
focus for industries worldwide, including the soybean processing industry. Ensuring environmentally 
friendly practices in cultivation and processing is essential to meet regulatory standards and public 
expectations. However, adapting to sustainable practices often requires significant investment, which 
can be a challenge for smaller processing units. Environmental concerns, such as deforestation and soil 
degradation linked to soybean cultivation, may also pose risks to the industry's reputation and long-
term viability. 
6. Raw Material Availability Risk: The soybean processing industry is highly dependent on the timely 
and adequate availability of soybeans, which is influenced by seasonal production patterns, monsoon 
performance, and acreage under cultivation. Any fluctuation in crop output due to adverse weather 
conditions, pest attacks, or shifts in farmer preference toward other remunerative crops can lead to raw 
material shortages. Limited domestic availability often results in higher procurement costs or increased 
reliance on imports, which may not always be viable due to import duties and global price volatility. 
Such disruptions can affect capacity utilization and profitability for processors.

4.10 Trend of Average Annual Domestic Soybean Oil Prices 
 
India's soybean oil prices have exhibited a clear upward trend with significant volatility, increasing from USD 
1,160/tonne in FY19 to USD 1,564/tonne in FY26, representing an overall increase of around 35%. Prices 
increased sharply during FY20–FY22, rising from USD 1,219/tonne to a peak of USD 1,749/tonne in FY22. 
The sharp increase during this period was supported by tight global edible oil supplies, higher commodity prices 
and elevated international soybean oil prices. Prices subsequently corrected to USD 1,569/tonne in FY23 and 
further to USD 1,361/tonne in FY24 as supply conditions improved and global edible oil prices moderated. 
 
The market regained momentum thereafter, with prices increasing to USD 1,550/tonne in FY25 and USD 
1,564/tonne in FY26, indicating a renewed firming of soybean oil prices. The relatively high price level in 
FY26, despite the correction from the FY22 peak, reflects the continued influence of India's structural import 
dependence, domestic soybean availability and international edible oil prices. India's soybean oil imports 
increased significantly in recent years, further strengthening the linkage between domestic prices and global 
markets. 
 
From a market perspective, higher soybean oil prices can improve realisations for soybean processors and 
support the value of the domestic processing market but simultaneously increase input costs for food 
manufacturers and put pressure on consumer prices. Going forward, prices are likely to remain sensitive to 
domestic soybean production and crushing volumes, global soybean availability, palm and sunflower oil prices, 
import duties, currency movements and biofuel demand, making price volatility an important consideration for 
participants across the soybean value chain.

5.3 Applications and Usages 
 
1. Food & Beverage Industry:  
Lecithin plays a critical role in the food and beverage industry, primarily as an emulsifier. It is widely used in 
products such as chocolates, margarine, baked goods, and instant food items to improve texture, moisture 
retention, and overall shelf life. By enabling the blending of fat and water, lecithin ensures consistent quality 
and mouthfeel in processed and convenience foods, making it a key ingredient in modern food formulations. 
The growing preference for Non-GMO lecithin, particularly for food applications across several European and 
Southeast Asian markets, is creating additional opportunities for Indian producers and exporters. Given the 
increasing demand for Non-GMO ingredients in these markets, the shift towards Non-GMO lecithin is expected 
to support the growth of India's lecithin exports and provide scope for further expansion in value-added soybean 
products. 
2. Pharmaceuticals: In the pharmaceutical sector, lecithin serves as a stabilizer and emulsifier, helping to 
enhance the bioavailability of active ingredients in drug formulations. It is particularly valuable in liposomal 
drug delivery systems, which are designed for efficient absorption. Lecithin is also commonly used in the 
production of soft gelatin capsules and nutritional supplements, where it helps in forming a stable and uniform 
dosage form. 
3. Cosmetics & Personal Care: Lecithin is frequently incorporated into skincare and personal care products 
due to its hydrating and skin-repairing properties. It functions as a moisturizing agent and emulsion stabilizer in 
creams, lotions, and serums, improving product texture and enhancing the delivery of active ingredients to the 
skin. Its natural origin also aligns with the growing demand for gentle, skin-friendly formulations. 
4. Animal Feed: In the animal feed industry, lecithin is used to improve digestibility and nutrient absorption. It 
serves as a valuable source of phospholipids and energy, especially in feed formulations for poultry and

6 COTTON SEED PROCESSING INDUSTRY IN INDIA 
 
6.1 Indian Cotton Seed Processing Industry 
 
The Indian cottonseed processing industry is crucial for producing cottonseed oil, meal, and hulls, supporting 
sectors like edible oils, animal feed, and paper production. With India being a major cotton producer, the 
industry benefits from rising demand for these products. However, it faces challenges such as fluctuating cotton 
production and waste disposal issues. Government policies and infrastructure investments continue to support its 
growth. 
  
The Government of India has introduced several initiatives to support the cotton spinning and textile sectors. 
These include reforms under a Special Package offering incentives for technology upgrades, tax relaxations, and 
fixed-term employment in the apparel sector. 
 
-The Market Access Initiative (MAI) Scheme launched in 2003 provides rebates and support for exporters.  
-The SAMARTH Scheme launched in 2017-18 aims to train 10 lakh workers to address labor shortages.  
-The Cott-Ally app launched in 2023 assists cotton farmers with MSP, procurement, and farming practices.  
-The Mega Investment Textile Parks (MITRA) scheme launched in 2021 planned to establish seven parks to 
boost global competitiveness, employment, and investment.  
The Indian government supports the cottonseed processing market through the PLI Scheme, boosting 
investment and efficiency in food processing. The Digital Agriculture Mission promotes AI and IoT for better 
productivity and supply chain management. Initiatives like NMEO-OP and farmer subsidies aim to enhance 
oilseed processing and reduce import dependence. Improved irrigation, research, and financial incentives further 
drive industry growth.

6.3 Key Trend & Growth Drivers  
 
Cotton cultivation in India significantly drives the growth of the cottonseed processing market. As one of the 
world’s top cotton producers, India's expanded cotton farming increases the availability of raw cottonseed, 
fueling market growth and supporting related industries. 
 
• 
Increase in Cotton Cultivation: India’s dominance in global cotton production drives the cottonseed 
processing market. The boost in cotton cultivation increases the demand for processed products like 
cottonseed oil, fueling the growth of processing operations. 
 
• 
Cottonseed as a Byproduct of Cotton Cultivation: Cottonseed byproducts, including cottonseed oil 
and cake, are vital for India’s edible oil and animal feed industries. Increased cotton cultivation boosts 
the supply of cottonseed, supporting the growth of the edible oil sector. Cottonseed cake, used as 
animal feed, and cottonseed meal, rich in protein, also drive demand in India’s expanding dairy and 
meat industries. 
 
• 
Technological Advancements and Enhanced Yield: The adoption of high-yield varieties, like Bt 
cotton hybrids, has increased cotton yields in India, expanding cultivation into less fertile areas. While 
India's lint yield ranks 33rd globally, technological advancements are expected to boost productivity. 
These improvements enhance cottonseed quality and quantity, benefiting manufacturers.  
 
6.4 Key Risks & Challenges  
 
Dependence on Monsoon: The cottonseed processing market in India is constrained by its dependence on 
monsoon rains, which impact cotton yields. Erratic weather, such as delayed or insufficient rainfall, can reduce 
cottonseed availability, driving up prices and creating market uncertainty. This deters small processors and 
limits industry growth. Additionally, reliance on traditional farming practices and lack of advanced irrigation 
systems worsen vulnerability to weather fluctuations. 
 
Limited Access to Credit: Limited access to credit is a major barrier for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) 
in India’s cottonseed processing market. The capital-intensive nature of the industry, combined with stringent 
lending requirements, prevents processors from investing in advanced equipment, expanding operations, and 
innovating. This results in inefficiencies and reduced competitiveness. Government support through subsidies, 
low-interest loans, and credit reforms is crucial to unlock the sector’s potential. 
 
6.5 Trend of Average Annual Domestic Cotton Seed Oil Prices  
 
Cottonseed oil price fluctuations in India are driven by several key factors. Weather patterns and agricultural 
output are primary, as cotton production depends on monsoon conditions, impacting supply. Global edible oil 
market conditions, including shortages in palm or soybean oil, also impact cottonseed oil prices, particularly 
during geopolitical tensions or supply chain disruptions. Further, international trade policies, including tariffs

241 
and export regulations, affect global flows and thus domestic pricing, particularly as demand from neighboring 
countries changes.

Cotton-seed oil prices declined from USD 1,080/ton in CY19 to USD 1,050/ton in CY20, reflecting weaker

trajectory, increasing to USD 1,130/ton in CY21 and USD 1,200/ton in CY22, supported by recovery in food 
and industrial demand, higher edible-oil prices and elevated input costs. The upward trend continued, albeit at a 
slower pace, with prices reaching USD 1,250/ton in CY23 and USD 1,270/ton in CY24 as supply remained

In CY25, prices increased further to USD 1,295/ton, while CY26P is estimated at USD 1,321/ton, indicating

in subsequent years suggests that the market is moving towards a more stable pricing environment, with 
cottonseed availability, global edible-oil prices, cotton production and processing economics expected to remain 
the key factors influencing price movements.

million by FY29. The segment is expected to grow at approximately 18.6% CAGR during FY26–FY29, 
supported by increasing demand for convenient and nutritionally enhanced plant-based protein products. Its 
relatively small base provides considerable headroom for expansion, particularly as manufacturers introduce 
differentiated flavour profiles and fortification with vitamins, minerals and other nutrients. Despite its relatively 
high growth rate, the category is expected to remain the smallest product segment in absolute market value 
through FY29.

9.3 Industry by Application

249 
Household / Retail Cooking: Household and retail cooking is the largest application for soya chunks and 
granules, increasing from Rs 5.07 billion in FY19 to Rs 12.72 billion in FY26 and projected to reach Rs 17.10 
billion by FY29. The segment benefits from the widespread use of soya products as an affordable, protein-rich 
ingredient in vegetarian household diets. Growing awareness of protein intake, affordability relative to other 
protein sources and established consumer familiarity are expected to support continued adoption. The segment is 
projected to grow at approximately 10.4% CAGR during FY26–FY29, remaining the dominant application 
despite faster growth in emerging end uses. 
Foodservice, HoReCa & Institutional Nutrition: Foodservice, HoReCa and institutional nutrition applications 
increased from Rs 1.15 billion in FY19 to Rs 3.01 billion in FY26 and are projected to reach Rs 4.16 billion by 
FY29, representing a 11.5% CAGR during FY26–FY29. Demand is supported by increasing use of soya 
products in restaurants, canteens, hostels, catering operations and institutional meal programmes, where 
affordability and ease of preparation are key advantages. Expansion of organised foodservice and institutional 
catering, together with growing demand for economical protein-rich meal options, is expected to drive further 
market growth. 
Processed / RTE–RTC Food Manufacturing: Processed and ready-to-eat/ready-to-cook food manufacturing 
is one of the faster-growing applications, increasing from Rs 0.71 billion in FY19 to Rs 2.36 billion in FY26 and 
projected to reach Rs 3.68 billion by FY29. The segment is expected to register a 15.9% CAGR during FY26–
FY29, supported by rising demand for convenience foods, packaged vegetarian products and protein-enriched 
ready-to-cook meals. Increasing urbanisation, changing consumption patterns and expansion of India's packaged 
food industry are encouraging manufacturers to incorporate soya chunks and granules into processed 
formulations, creating additional demand beyond traditional household consumption. 
Plant-based Meat & Meat Extenders: Plant-based meat and meat-extender applications represent a smaller 
but rapidly expanding segment, increasing from Rs 0.19 billion in FY19 to Rs 1.13 billion in FY26 and 
projected to reach Rs 2.14 billion by FY29. The segment is expected to grow at approximately 23.7% CAGR 
during FY26–FY29, the fastest among the major applications. Growth is being driven by increasing consumer 
interest in plant-based protein, product innovation and development of vegetarian and meat-alternative products 
using textured soy protein. Although the current market base remains relatively small, the rapid growth indicates 
significant potential for soya chunks and granules as functional meat extenders and protein ingredients in 
modern food formulations. 
Animal & Pet Feed: Animal and pet feed applications, including feed-grade textured soy protein, increased 
from Rs 0.34 billion in FY19 to Rs 0.95 billion in FY26 and are projected to reach Rs 1.43 billion by FY29, 
corresponding to a 14.5% CAGR during FY26–FY29. Demand is supported by the protein requirements of 
livestock and pet nutrition formulations, with textured soy products providing a relatively economical plant-
based protein source. The segment is expected to benefit from growth in organised animal nutrition and pet food 
markets, although its overall contribution remains smaller than human food applications. Its comparatively 
strong projected growth also reflects increasing utilisation of processed soy protein in specialised feed 
formulations.

10 Analysis of End User Industries 
 
India’s key industries, including animal feed, food and beverages, personal care, and pharmaceuticals, are 
witnessing strong growth driven by rising consumer demand, favorable government policies, and shifts towards 
innovation and sustainability.

250 
• 
Animal Feed 
India’s livestock sector exhibits a nuanced trajectory influenced by shifting economic needs and regulatory 
measures. In the animal feed industry, India’s expanding livestock and dairy sectors are boosting feed demand, 
particularly for poultry, aquaculture, and dairy animals. Growth in dairy, poultry, and fisheries is primarily 
driven by rising domestic consumption and technological advancements. Recent regulatory changes emphasize 
sustainability and animal welfare, encouraging the sector to adopt more ethical practices. The future of India’s 
livestock industry appears favorable, backed by government policies, regulatory reforms, and stable demand, 
solidifying its role as a vital element in the country’s agricultural and economic framework. The segment is 
expected to grow from Rs 318 billion in FY26 to Rs 372 billion by FY29 at a CAGR of 5.4%.  
 
• 
Food & Beverages 
 
India's food and beverage sector are rapidly expanding, fueled by shifts in consumer tastes, urban growth, and a 
stronger emphasis on health and sustainability. Key trends include a growing appetite for convenient foods, 
organic products, plant-based alternatives, and health-oriented beverages. Technology and e-commerce are 
reshaping consumer access to these products, making the industry increasingly diverse and accessible. This 
sector’s growth is propelled by rising incomes, urbanization, and changing dietary preferences favoring 
packaged and health-conscious products. The segment is expected to grow from Rs 85 billion in FY26 to Rs 100 
billion by FY29 at a CAGR of 5.8%. 
 
• 
Personal Care 
 
In the personal care industry, India is seeing an accelerated demand for premium, natural, and herbal products. 
Consumers are increasingly conscious of sustainable and ethical choices, and e-commerce is driving much of 
industry’s growth. The fast-moving personal care segment is a vital contributor to India’s GDP. It caters to the 
daily needs of individuals which range from essential food items having an inelastic demand such as soap, 
shampoo, detergent, etc. The personal care industry is projected to have a positive outlook in the near-to-
medium term with increased brand consciousness, favorable demographics, rise in disposable income, 
urbanization, a growing number of supermarkets, an uptick in the consumption of high-quality branded 
products. The segment is expected to grow from Rs 28 billion in FY26 to Rs 34 billion by FY29 at a CAGR of 
6.5%. 
 
• 
Pharmaceuticals 
 
The Indian pharmaceutical industry (IPI) is ranked 3rd globally in volume and 14th in value. The lower market 
share in terms of value can be attributed to the predominance of IPI in generic medicines (accounting for about 
70% of the industry’s revenues) which command lower prices. The segment is expected to grow from Rs 18 
billion in FY26 to Rs 23 billion by FY29 at a CAGR of 7.0%. 
 
Growth in the domestic pharmaceutical market is expected to be driven by increased penetration of health 
insurance, improved access to healthcare facilities, rising prevalence of chronic diseases, and rising per capita 
income. The export growth is expected to be led by increasing generic penetration in the regulated markets on 
the back of enhanced focus on the niche and complex product segments, patent expiries, medicine patent pool 
announcing licensing agreements with pharmaceutical companies, and growing demand from semi-regulated 
pharma markets. In the long term, growth in the export market will be sustained by emerging markets such as 
Russia, Brazil, and South Africa, etc. 
 
• 
Pharma Exports 
 
Pharma exports from India mainly comprise four broad categories with a lion’s share coming from drug 
formulations, and biologicals. During the FY26, the segment drug formulations, and biologicals accounted for a 
significant share of 78.0% followed by bulk drugs, drug intermediates (APIs), Ayush and herbal products, and 
surgical with a contribution of 17.2%, 2.3%, and 2.5%, respectively. Exports of drug formulations and 
biologicals to the USA witnessed 6.2% growth primarily due to price erosion in the USA.  
 
11 THREATS AND CHALLENGES

251 
Volatility in Soybean Prices and Availability – Soybean is the primary raw material for soybean crushing and 
processing, making processors highly exposed to fluctuations in procurement prices. Prices are influenced by 
domestic production, acreage, monsoon conditions, crop yields, farmer selling patterns and global soybean 
prices. Significant price movements can increase working-capital requirements and adversely affect crushing 
margins, particularly when processors are unable to pass higher raw-material costs through to soybean oil and 
meal realisations. 
High Dependence on Imported Edible Oils – India remains structurally dependent on imports to meet a 
significant portion of its edible oil consumption. This exposes the domestic industry to international oil prices, 
exchange-rate fluctuations, freight costs and geopolitical or supply-chain disruptions. Sharp movements in 
global palm, soybean and sunflower oil prices can influence domestic price realisations and create uncertainty 
for processors in managing inventories and procurement. 
Thin and Volatile Crushing Margins – Soybean processing profitability is primarily determined by the 
relationship between soybean procurement costs and the combined realisations from soybean oil and soybean 
meal. Changes in the relative prices of these by-products can significantly alter the crush spread. Consequently, 
even periods of strong demand may not translate into higher profitability if raw-material prices increase faster 
than oil and meal realisations. 
Government Policy and Regulatory Changes – The industry is sensitive to changes in import duties, tariff 
structures, stock limits, export regulations, minimum support prices and other government interventions. 
Changes in import duties on edible oils, in particular, can alter import parity and domestic price 
competitiveness. Frequent or unexpected policy changes can also make procurement, inventory management 
and capacity planning more challenging for processors. 
Climate and Monsoon-related Risks – Domestic soybean production is highly dependent on monsoon 
conditions, particularly in major producing states such as Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan. Erratic 
rainfall, droughts, excessive precipitation and changing climatic conditions can affect acreage, crop yields and 
soybean quality. A weaker domestic crop can tighten raw-material availability, increase procurement costs and 
adversely affect capacity utilisation of processing facilities. 
Competition from Imported Products – Domestic processors face competition from imported edible oils as 
well as soybean meal and other processed soybean products. When international prices are favourable, imported 
products can become competitive with domestically produced products, putting pressure on domestic 
realisations. This is particularly relevant for processors operating with higher procurement, logistics or 
processing costs than international suppliers. 
Rising Operating, Logistics and Storage Costs – Processing companies are exposed to increases in electricity, 
fuel, transportation, labour, warehousing and other operating expenses. Soybean is also a seasonal commodity, 
requiring adequate storage and inventory management to ensure year-round processing. Higher logistics and 
storage costs, combined with increased working-capital requirements during periods of elevated soybean prices, 
can further pressure margins and overall processing economics. 
 
12 COMPETITIVE LANDSCAPE 
 
12.1 Business Profile  
 
Maharashtra Oil Extraction Ltd. (MOEL) is a Maharashtra based company engaged in the processing of 
soybeans and production of soybean-based products. The company operates three manufacturing plants- Dhule, 
Gangakhed & Nandurbar located in Maharashtra, one of the country’s largest soybean-producing states, which 
contributes around 47.3% of India’s total output. This strategic location provides MOEL with direct access to 
key raw material sources, ensuring supply reliability and cost efficiency. 
  
MOEL’s product portfolio spans the entire soybean value chain, including solvent-extracted soybean oil, refined 
edible oil, food grade soya lecithin, high-protein soymeal, and value-added products such as toasted and 
untoasted soya flour, soya flakes, and textured soya protein. The company exports to 19+ countries and is the 
largest exporter of soya toasted flakes in terms of volume.   
 
The company’s refined edible oil operations consistently maintain capacity utilization above 60%, well above 
the industry average of below 50%, reflecting operational efficiency and strong process management. The 
Company’s manufacturing facilities are strategically located to optimise the sourcing of raw materials and 
enable efficient logistics management. The manufacturing facilities are located within 200–300 km of the 
soybean production belts of Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, which account for 47.3%, 2.2% and 
39.1%, respectively, of the country’s total soybean seed production. This proximity enables the Company to 
procure soybean seed, its largest raw material, at competitive prices while reducing inbound freight costs. 
Further, the strategic location of the manufacturing facilities provides the Company with access to key ports,

252 
including Jawaharlal Nehru Port in Mumbai, Maharashtra and Hazira Port in Surat, Gujarat, facilitating efficient 
outbound logistics and supporting the Company’s ability to serve international markets. 
 
Over the years, MOEL has built a consistent customer base, generating approximately 85% of its revenue from 
repeat customers, highlighting trust and alignment with customer expectations. The company has also been 
awarded as the “Third Highest Sale of Soybean Refined Oil in Consumer Pack”, “Second Highest Exporter of 
Soy Value Added Products” and “Third Highest Soybean Processing” by The Soybean Processors Association 
of India (“SOPA”) at its SOPA International Conclave held on October 08 and 09, 2025.

OVERVIEW 
 
We are in the business of processing, manufacturing, marketing and sale of various products across the soya bean 
products value chain, including crude and edible refined oil, plant based protein supplement for feed and food 
grade soya meal, value-added products like soya flour and Textured Soya Protein (“TSP”) and byproducts such as 
lecithin and other speciality and industrial chemicals. We produce and market food grade soya meal products such 
as non-GMO defatted toasted and untoasted soya flakes and grits in domestic and international market to 
manufacturers of Soya sauce, TSP and other Food products. In addition, we are also engaged in the business of 
refining and sale of cottonseed oil. We are also in the field of manufacturing of Sunflower oil wherein we 
purchase refined sunflower oil add additive and pack it in different SKUs for sale. We majorly distribute, sell and 
market our edible soya bean oil and cottonseed oil in the domestic market under our owned brand “Murli”. We 
produce and market our feed grade soya meal products containing protein ranging from 46% to 50% & full fat 
meal with protein content of approximately 38% under the brand “MOEL” for aqua and feed industry. This feed 
grade soya meal is produced for both domestic and international market. For the Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, we 
exported 49,282.32 MT, 40,270.27 MT and 36,637.07 MT, respectively of soya flakes, which is primarily used 
for the production of soya sauce. We are India’s largest exporter of food grade toasted soya flakes in terms of 
volume. (source: CARE Report) Further, in recognition of our performance and contribution to the soy processing 
industry, we have been conferred the awards for ‘Third Highest Sale of Soybean Refined Oil in Consumer Pack’, 
‘Second Highest Exporter of Soy Value Added Products’, and ‘Third Highest Soybean Processing’ by the 
Soybean Processors Association of India (“SOPA”) in the year 2025 (source: CARE Report). 
 
As a part of our forward integrated business model, the derived products from our soya bean processing cycle 
namely non-GMO defatted toasted and untoasted soya flakes and grits are utilized by, our subsidiary, Basant 
Nutrifoods Private Limited (“BNPL”) for production and marketing of value-added products like soya flour and 
TSP in domestic and international market. Over the years, we have grown from a small-scale soya bean 
processing business to a key player in the edible oil and soya protein food grade products through strategic 
capacity expansions, technological upgrades, strengthening of our quality control systems, continuous product 
development, research & development initiatives and focused efforts towards diversification into high-value 
products.

10. Return on Net Worth is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the period / year divided by average net worth. Net

deducting the aggregate value of the accumulated losses, deferred expenditure and miscellaneous expenditure not 
written off, as per the restated statement of assets and liabilities, but does not include reserves created out of 
revaluation of assets, write-back of depreciation and amalgamation. Average net worth is the sum of opening and 
closing balance of net worth for relevant fiscal divided by two. 
11. Return on capital employed (ROCE) is calculated as EBIT divided by closing capital employed for the period / fiscal 
year. Earnings before Interest and Taxes (EBIT) is calculated as restated profit / (loss) for the period / fiscal year, plus 
finance costs and total taxes. Capital employed is the sum of total equity plus debt consisting of borrowings and lease 
liabilities plus deferred tax liabilities less deferred tax assets, as appearing in the Restated Financial Information. 
12. Trade receivables days are calculated as Average Trade receivables divided by Revenue from operations and 
multiplied by number of days in the fiscal year. Average trade receivables is the sum of opening and closing balance of 
trade receivables for relevant fiscal divided by two. 
13. Inventory days are calculated as Average Inventory divided by Revenue from operations and multiplied by number of 
days in the fiscal year. Average Inventory is the sum of opening and closing balance of Inventory for relevant fiscal 
divided by two. 
14. Working Capital days is the sum of Inventory days and Trade Receivables days subtracted by Trade Payables days. 
Trade payables days are calculated as Average Trade payables divided by Revenue from operations and multiplied by 
number of days in the fiscal year. Average trade payables is the sum of opening and closing balance of trade payables 
for relevant fiscal divided by two.

Our business is working capital intensive, primarily due to the seasonal nature of the agri-processing industry. 
During the peak periods, spanning the Kharif and Rabi seasons from October to March, we experience higher 
raw material supply and customer demand, necessitating larger inventories of both raw materials and finished 
goods. To minimise the exposure of our operations to seasonal impact, we maintain a robust approach to 
managing receivables, ensuring that we consistently have fewer receivables from debtors. This focus on 
minimizing outstanding receivables is a critical element of our efficient working capital management strategy. 
Given the scale of our operations and the continuous growth of our customer base, maintaining adequate 
inventory levels is essential. As a result, our business consistently requires substantial working capital support to 
ensure smooth and uninterrupted operations and hedge for the forward export & domestic contracts. We achieve 
this by establishing clear credit policies, conducting thorough due diligence of potential customers, and 
maintaining strong relationships with our clients. These efforts help ensure that payments are received on time 
and that any overdue accounts are promptly addressed. Additionally, we actively monitor and manage accounts 
receivable turnover, which helps us identify any potential issues early and mitigate the risk of non-payment or 
delayed payments. By reducing the amount of receivables outstanding, we not only improve our cash flow but 
also enhance our ability to reinvest in the business, meet our financial obligations, and ensure sustainable 
growth. These effective receivables management supports our financial stability and further strengthens our 
reputation as a reliable and financially sound entity. 
 
This is attributable to our continued focus on product quality and process improvement, diversification of 
product portfolio, competitive pricing and cost rationalization. Our strong financial performance in past reflects 
the efficacy of the processing, manufacturing and management protocols that we have implemented and strong

seed crushing. This has been validated through technical specifications, on-site layout verification, and historical 
operational records. It is important to note that the stated capacity refers to processing of raw material (soybean seed). 
The plant is designed to produce both animal feed-grade soya meal and human edible food-grade toasted and untoasted 
products known as value-added toasted products. While the capacity remains close to 500 MTPD during production of 
general-grade soya meal, it effectively reduces to approximately 400 MTPD when processing toasted, value-added 
variants due to longer retention time and additional processing requirements. This operational shift may reflect as

Raw Materials and Suppliers 
 
The key raw materials used in the manufacturing of our major products include soya bean. Historically, we have 
sourced raw materials from multiple vendors in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat.  
 
• 
Soyabean seeds: The principal raw material required for manufacturing our products is ‘soya bean seeds’. 
Soya bean seeds are procured directly from the farmers or through traders / agents or from auction centres 
(mandis) from state of Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat. Occasionally, we also import non-GMO 
soya bean seed from Africa. Majority of our soya bean seed requirement is purchased and procured 
directly from the farmers through direct procurement centres / agents. Our senior management team 
(including our promoters) personally oversees the sourcing of oilseeds at various centres. These direct 
procurement centres reduces dependence on the mandi/agent system and thus their intermediation margins. 
Our Manufacturing Facilities also comprises warehouses, storage silos with a combined capacity of 35,000 
MT and two (2) storage bins with a combined capacity of 1,060 MT for storage of soya bean seeds. 
 
• 
Soya crude oil: We also procure soya crude oil from various other solvent extraction plant for refining 
purpose. 
 
• 
Wash cotton seed oil: For refining cotton seed oil, we procure the cotton crude oil from local small oil 
mills and traders.  
 
• 
Untoasted flakes/ Grits: Our subsidiary, BNPL manufactures toasted/untoasted soya flour from 
toasted/untoasted flakes/ grits which procured from our Company.

300 
• 
Chemicals and solvents: Various chemicals and solvents like (i) hexane for extraction of crude oil and (ii) 
bleaching earth, caustic soda, citric acid, phosphoric acid, are used in the process of solvent extraction and 
refining. These are sourced from domestic vendors of these products. 
 
• 
Boiler fuel: Each of our processing plants has a steam boiler. Our boilers are primarily dependent on agro 
waste fuel such as corn cob and sugar cane bagasse, which are procured locally from farmers and traders. 
 
• 
Packaging material is required especially for packaging, retailing and branding of products. Material such 
as polypropylene bags, metal tins and jars are sourced from various suppliers locally. We label these 
packages attractively to enable the consumer recognise our products amongst other products. The label 
also provides the details of the products like ingredients, weight, quality etc. as required under law. We 
focus on ensuring that the packaging of our products is both attractive and ergonomically designed to 
appeal to retail consumers. 
 
For the Fiscals 2026, 2025 and 2024, our combined cost of materials consumed and purchase of stock in trade 
was ₹ 19,931.03 million, ₹ 16,793.34 million and ₹ 16,275.33 million representing 90.12%, 89.17% and 93.27% 
of our total revenue from operations, respectively. We usually do not enter into long-term supply contracts with 
any of our raw material suppliers and typically source raw materials from third-party suppliers or open market. 
The terms and conditions for product quality and return policy are set forth in the purchase orders. Pricing and 
production volumes are negotiated for each purchase order. There are no contractual commitments other than 
those set forth in the purchase orders. The purchase price of our raw materials generally follows market prices. 
However, we maintain good relationships with our suppliers and have, where possible, diversified our supplier 
base so as to avoid a disruption in supply. Further we are also preferred by our seed suppliers, as we prioritize 
timely payments, preferred pricing, and a smooth procurement process, all of which help strengthen our supply 
chain. By ensuring prompt payment for deliveries, we build trust and reliability with our suppliers, which often 
leads to better terms and preferential pricing. This commitment to timely transactions allows us to access 
competitive pricing and secure favorable conditions for future purchases. Moreover, by streamlining the 
procurement process, including clear communication and consistent ordering patterns, we minimize delays and 
maintain steady supply levels. This approach not only ensures that we have a reliable flow of high-quality raw 
materials but also supports long-term relationships with suppliers, which further stabilizes our supply chain and 
mitigates risks of disruption. No single supplier or third-party producer accounts for a material portion of our 
purchases or business. We typically purchase raw materials based on the historical levels of sales, actual sales 
orders on hand and the anticipated sales forecasting taking into consideration any expected fluctuation in raw 
material prices and delivery delay. 
 
Additionally, the prices of our raw materials are also based on, or linked to, the international price of such raw 
materials and the variations are typically passed on to the customers, which helps reduce the impact of volatility 
in the prices on our margins. Raw material price fluctuations are mitigated through formula-based pricing; our 
products typically have a fixed and a variable price component and the variable component is linked to the price 
of the commodity on international markets.  
 
Inventory management  
 
Our finished products are stored on-site at our Manufacturing Facilities. We generally store sufficient stock of 
finished goods and raw materials at our Manufacturing Facilities at our owned warehousing facilities which also 
comprises warehouses, storage silos with a combined capacity of 35,000 MT and two (2) storage bins with a 
combined capacity of 1,060 MT for storage of soya bean seeds or outsourced warehousing facilities. 
Additionally, we also have tanks for storage of refined vegetable oil, soya and cotton crude oil with a combined 
capacity of 5,650 MT. We produce a quantity of finished products that is determined based on a combination of 
confirmed and expected orders. Our expected orders have historically been confirmed due to the stable long-
standing relationships that we have with our direct customers and dealers. Our production and inventory levels 
of our finished products are planned on a periodic basis based on the projected sales volumes and we make 
periodic adjustments to the production schedule and volumes based on actual orders received. We closely 
supervise our daily production and aim to maintain suitable inventory levels of raw materials and finished goods 
at each of our Manufacturing Facilities. Further, for raw materials, we maintain different inventory levels 
depending on lead time required to obtain additional supplies.

Utilities 
 
All our operating facilities have access to the necessary utilities like hexane, electricity, fuel and water. As a part 
of the oil extraction and refining process, we consume a high amount of power and steam. Our power 
requirements are mostly met through supply from Maharashtra State Electricity Board. We have also installed a 
solar power plant at our manufacturing facility at Gangakhed, Maharashtra with an installed capacity of 651.98 
KW. Further, to reduce the production wastage during the interruption in our electricity requirements, each of 
our processing plants also has a backup diesel generator. Our steam requirements are fulfilled by our steam 
boilers. Each of our processing plants has a steam boiler. Our boilers are primarily dependent on agrowaste fuel 
such as corn cobb and sugar cane bagasse, which is procured local farmers, traders and sugar factories. Our 
water requirements are met though supplies from MIDC. In case of shortage of water supplies, we avail 
facilities from local water tanker supplier. We also source the water supply from, municipal supply, water tanker 
and bore wells for our manufacturing facility at Nandurbar, Maharashtra. Furthermore, Gangakhed 
Manufacturing Facility has access to water through two borewells located at the manufacturing facility. 
Additionally, water is also sourced via a dedicated 1 km pipeline from private farmers in the vicinity of our 
Gangakhed Manufacturing facility. Water is mainly used to generate steam as required in the manufacturing 
process of our products. We have also installed RO plant/water softener at our Manufacturing Facilities for 
process water and drinking water.
